Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I do so with a keen awareness of the responsibilities vested in me by the people in the Kindersley constituency to present their views in the parliament of Canada. There are two problems that I shall deal with at this time, and there are many others that I shall be mentioning later when time and circumstances permit.
As a new member, I have found some difficulty in becoming accustomed to parliamentary rules and procedures, as well as becoming accustomed to the routine in the city of Ottawa. Upon my arrival I was fortunate enough to meet a friend who showed me the various points of interest in the city. Since I saw him last he had been married and I was naturally rather solicitous of his welfare.
I asked him how he was getting along and he told me he was having quite a hard time making ends meet because of the high cost of living. In addition, he said he had a very extravagant wife. I was naturally concerned, so I questioned him further. He said, "Well, shortly after we were married she asked me for $50; the next day she asked for $50 and a while later for $100. She is always asking for money." I said, "Well, my goodness, what does she do with it all?" He said, "I do not know; I never give her any."
Judging from what I have learned about this government, Mr. Speaker, we are likely to hear much more in these proceedings about a livestock marketing board and the problem of advance payments on farm-stored grain.
I should like to describe the conditions which have resulted from the failure of this government to heed the advice of farmers, farm unions and farm organizations to set up a livestock marketing board. I believe that we are generally aware of the hazards of livestock production, particularly those of us who come from western Canada. We are familiar with the hazards of drought and the failure of feed production, and the devastations of disease in the herd or flock. When we are


faced with these hazards, plus the hazard of price manipulation at the will of the large packing houses, we are faced with a situation which has forced farmers out of livestock production.
For example, in the Saskatoon market the average prices for the week ending June 23, 1951, were as follows: Choice steers, $34.50 and common cows, $23.75. A little over two years later, for the week ending September 19, 1953, choice steers were selling at $18 and common cows at $7.30. Those are not necessarily the high and the low in the prices, but are representative figures which I have selected more or less at random. The current review for November, 1953, points out that hog gradings in Saskatchewan were reduced from 1,077,000 in 1943-47 to 430,842 in 1952. Egg production in Saskatchewan has decreased from 53,567,000 dozen in 1943-47 to
32.312.000	dozen in 1952. On the other hand, wheat acreage has increased in Saskatchewan from 12,977,000 acres in the period 1943-47 to
16.100.000	acres in 1953. It seems apparent then, Mr. Speaker, since western farmers are hard-headed businessmen, that they have found that they are unable to remain in the livestock business with these fluctuations in price.
A similar situation existed for many years in connection with the marketing of wheat when we were left to the mercies of the Winnipeg grain exchange. After many years of pressure the Canadian Wheat Board Act was introduced on June 10, 1935, by those friends of free enterprise, the Conservative government. It was not until September, 1943, that the present government saw fit to utilize these powers to the fullest advantage, but they have continued to neglect placing rye and flax under the wheat board. The marketing of these grains is left to these wolves of free enterprise, the Winnipeg grain exchange.
Farmers have been granted some security in the production of wheat, and the other part of their program, the livestock production, has failed to receive any notice. Farmers, therefore, have gone out of livestock and put the acreages that they would normally devote to that into wheat. Since they have become in many cases straight grain farmers, there is no necessity for staying on the farm in the long winter months; consequently, many have moved to the towns and villages where they can enjoy some of the amenities of life other occupations take for granted.
With a density of population of around one per square mile in my area of Saskatchewan, and you find two or three farmers moving out of the district and into the towns and villages, your population then becomes so sparse that your school problem becomes

complicated; your municipal problem of building all-weather roads is intensified; your problem of rural electrification is greatly increased; and the social aspect is suffering and the local community centre is beginning to disappear. As a solution to these conditions, Mr. Speaker, it is necessary to establish a livestock marketing board, similar to the Canadian wheat board. I should like to see one major exception. I should like to see producer representation on this livestock marketing board, because it appears from our experience with the Canadian wheat board that once you fail to get producer representation you have a very difficult time indeed in achieving it.
I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the royal commission on price spreads of 1934 made the recommendation that a livestock marketing board be established; and, incidentally, these recommendations have been ignored by the government of Canada for the past 19 years. Some of the duties of the board which the royal commission recommends, and which I shall mention, are:
1.	An adequate inspection of all marketing stages and action to correct abuses.
It is interesting to point out, as the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) has done, that the packers have established the ability of grading our cattle with the arbitrary grade of choice, good, medium, common and so on. Meat is graded on a voluntary basis as to red brand, blue brand, commercial and so on, to assist consumers, and there is not necessarily any correspondence between the grades. A steer a farmer sold as a medium could conceivably be branded red label. I continue with the recommendations.
2.	Co-operation with producers, processors and the trade generally, to ensure as far as possible a balance between production and available markets.
3.	To encourage the organization of producers of livestock for regular and orderly marketing.
4.	The formation of a uniform policy on external marketing with a view not only to promoting new, but also retaining and developing, existing markets.
These are some of the duties as set out by the royal commission and they would serve to stabilize the markets by a system of forward pricing which would stabilize the agricultural economy in times of economic strain.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has made many excuses in his very capable manner, and doubtless with the support of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), who is "not a strong advocate of government in business", claiming that it is a provincial matter. Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of national importance, and on behalf of the people I represent I am demanding action.
The Address-Mr. W. M. Johnson
Largely because of the failure of the government to give security to livestock producers, and because of the failure to follow an aggressive policy of international trade, the problem of an immediate need for a policy of advance payments on farm-stored grain becomes more apparent. The Western Producer of November 19 states:
Referring to interim farm finance, Mr. Wesson recalled the wheat pool board had brought the matter to the attention of the federal government last August.
Further on we find:
He said Mr. Howe had not refused government assistance. The matter was being left until parliament assembled, Mr. Wesson had been assured.
I hope that the statement given to the house on November 18 by the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not considered as having the full advantage of parliamentary debate, and that it cannot be considered final.
The Current Review of November, 1953, states:
A major change in this year's income pattern is the significant decrease in agricultural income from the very high level of 1952. This year's grain crop, though exceptionally large, is below last year's record, and at the same time farm prices have continued the decline which began early in 1952.
Costs, on the other hand, have failed to drop. The index of goods and services used by the farmers has increased from 157 in 1946 to 243 in 1952. Factors contributing to this have been the high cost of fertilizer, the high cost of farm machinery and the high cost of farm storage, coupled with the freight rates-all matters which require investigation and action.
The matter was further complicated by the open quota in the pre-election period and the subsequent maldistribution of box cars. The result has been that some farmers have been able to get their quota marketed while others situated a greater distance from the market, or who did not know the quota was open, have been denied that privilege. The arbitrary cancellation of the car order book caused hardship in areas where it was operative. I think you will agree that the car order book is outdated. I therefore think it was the responsibility of the government not to cancel it but to substitute some other means of legislation which would permit the farmers to deliver grain to the elevators of their choice.
Costs of production must be considered when any statements are made that the farmers have received over $1 billion from the 1952 crop. I believe there would be considerable interest in the costs of farming, as we certainly cannot for one moment assume that the gross returns are the profits.

The Address-Mr, W. M. Johnson "A farm business study in the Fox Valley-Eston-Kindersley area of Saskatchewan," a major portion of my constituency, put out by the Department of Agriculture, points out that the average size of farm land class 3 is 587 acres, or just under a section. Class 3 refers to the productivity, with land class 1 being submarginal for wheat production, class 2 marginal, class 3 fair, class 4 good and class 5 excellent. It is significant that less than 40 per cent of the land in this area is class 3 or better. This study goes on to point out that the cash operating expenses on the average farm are $2,664, corrected to the increase in costs of goods and services used by the farmers which increased from 157 when the study was made to 243 last year. No allowance is made for depreciation, so that must be considered. Let us assume that the value of equipment is $10,000, a very low figure, which if depreciated at 10 per cent would give you $1,000. The average capital invested on a farm, land class 3, is $22,415, and the legitimate charge of interest on your investment at 5 per cent is $1,220. Therefore the total expenses on the farm are $4,884. The study goes on to point out that 47 per cent of the cropland is devoted to wheat, giving a wheat acreage of 276.
This gives us an actual cost of nearly $17.75 per wheat acre. It is to be pointed out that this figure does not include any returns to the operator; it does not include any returns for his family, nor does it include anything for the retirement of debt. Under the present cost of living I do not see how a family can expect to get along on less than $200 a month. If that is included, the cost per wheat acre becomes the very significant figure of $25.
In many cases the farmers were unable to market more than 20 bushels per acre which in my area would give them a return, at $1.21 for No. 1 northern, assuming they had the best grade, plus the 12 cent participation payment, of $26.60 per wheat acre. The Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that a payment on the 1952 crop would be made in 1954. This points out the crux of the whole problem. The farmers are being paid a year or two after their expenses have been incurred. The expenses for 1953 have been assumed and very little, if anything, has been received. The farmer is then forced to live on what meagre savings he may have.
I would like to ask hon. members of this house, what would be your reaction if you were told you were not going to receive anything for this year's work until next year at this time? That is just the position of the western grain grower.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce stated in the house on November 18:
Even so, grain has been moving off the farms into terminal positions and for export at a pretty fair rate. To judge from some of the comments I have heard one might get the impression that the grain movement had come to a stop. Nothing could be farther from the truth. In some respects the movement is at record levels.
The dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin of November 19 states:
Deliveries from prairie farms during the week were down to 7,510,000 from 11,673,000 a year ago, while the overseas export clearances declined to
2.973.000	from 6,628,000.
I do not think I need to add anything other than to point out that those statements do not seem to be compatible. It is obvious that the responsibility is upon the government to create legislation to allow those in financial need and who are unable to deliver grain to get relief. There are perhaps not too many that are suffering, but if there were only
1.000	farmers in need the legislation would still be required. This would also assist those who are dependent upon the farmer. It would assist the small retailer who has granted credit to the farmer knowing he had wheat and that in due time he will be able to market it.
I believe an advance payment of not less than 75 cents per bushel on at least 2,000 bushels would be the very minimum to meet the need. I would prefer to see this figure higher and more in relation to the recommendation of the Saskatchewan farm union. It would be a simple matter. As you know, under the Canadian Wheat Board Act every producer of wheat must have a permit book. This could be handled through the local elevator agent. If a farmer went to a local agent and asked for an advance, the money would be given to him and an entry made in his permit book.
When the time came when there was room in the elevator and the farmer was able to deliver grain the advance would be automatically deducted.
I would point out that this is aimed at assisting the smaller farmer and would cost the government only the interest on the money borrowed to make the advance. It would not be in the neighbourhood of millions of dollars, as has been stated in the press. The more fortunate would not require this advance. Those who have been able to deliver their quota would not require it. It is those who have been unable to market any grain that would require this assistance.
I do not want my statements to be construed as criticism of the Canadian wheat

board. In fact I think this shows its strength. It shows that it is able to be changed in order to meet current needs. I will conclude by stating that I believe I have proved the necessity for immediate action in the establishment of a livestock marketing board and the need and desirability of advance payment on farm-stored grain. These things are necessary to give security to agriculture, the base of our Canadian economy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the history of our times is written it will be remembered by future generations as the era of the three isms, fascism, communism and McCarthyism. I am not going to attempt to define the first two, but I think McCarthyism should be defined. I am prepared to accept the definition given by a former president of the United States who has lived in a close and intimate fashion with McCarthyism. Here is his definition as reported in the Globe and Mail of November 17:
It is the corruption of truth, the abandonment of our historical devotion to fair play.
It is the abandonment of the due process of law.
It is the use of the big lie and the unfounded accusation against any citizen in the name of Americanism or security.
It is the rise to power of the demagogue who lives on untruth.
It is the spread of fear and the destruction of faith in every level of our society.
The former president of the United States, Mr. Harry S. Truman, told the Americans to fight that evil at every level of their national life. These three pernicious philosophies have in common the same end and the same means. Their end is to confuse, to divide, to conquer and ultimately to enslave. Their means are the big lie and the big smear. They were born in the gutter and the first of them, fascism, has already died and has been buried in the gutter. We hope sincerely that the other two will share the same fate.
The two surviving isms have another element in common. If you attack either of them you are accused immediately of belonging to the other. Anyone who has the temerity to oppose McCarthyism runs the risk of being branded a communist. At least he will be in good company since even Robin Hood wears the red tassel and red label today.
The spectacle of what McCarthyism has done to our good neighbours to the south has been a source of sadness and concern to thinking people everywhere. No one will disagree that subversives in government are despicable and should be cleared out, as they have been in this country; but to do this in an atmosphere of popular hysteria and to make it a combination of witch hunt and
The Address-Mr. Croll a three-ringed circus is to debase the functions of democracy and prevent the carrying out of the true processes of law.
So long as McCarthyism stayed at home we remained silent on the principle that the domestic affairs of a country were that country's problem. But the situation has changed. The McCarthyites are no longer content to pour their malice on their fellow citizens; they want to throw mud across the border at Canada. They have singled out as their first candidate the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). The Globe and Mail of November 8 contains an article from New York headed, "U. S. Writer says Pearson Blocked Probe into Spying." Then it states:
Victor Lasky, former New York newspaperman-
And it continues:
-directed his attack chiefly at External Affairs Minister Pearson who he claimed has "consistently sabotaged" efforts to disclose soviet intrigue in Washington and Ottawa.
He went on to say that the minister had effectively squelched any investigation into alleged Soviet ties not only of his closest aide, but of himself. That was a statement made by a planted stooge attempting to make a smear. He knew his statement was false when he made it, but despite that he made it. But it is enough for our purpose. He has rung the alarm bell, the attack has now begun on the minister and it appears that it will be carried out by professionals. Mr. Lasky got his name into the headlines by implying that the minister was an ally of the Soviet fifth column. This little known journalist even tried to suggest, although he was careful to avoid entanglements with the libel laws, that the minister had provided information to one Elizabeth Bentley, a Soviet spy in Washington during the war. These charges, of course, are ludicrous. It is of course conceivable that Miss Bentley and some other spies quoted people who quoted people who quoted the minister, just as they might have quoted people who quoted people who quoted General Marshall or General Eisenhower. To be quoted and misquoted is the fate of those who are well known in political and diplomatic life.
The attack was not lost upon the press of this country and the people of this country. The Ottawa Citizen on November 19 carried a leading editorial "The Attack on Mr. Pearson":
Mud from the current American witch hunt has now been thrown across the border, with Mr. Pearson, the minister of external affairs, the target.
It goes on:
He helped found the United Nations, and has been a moving spirit in the formation of the North

The Address-Mr. Croll Atlantic Treaty Organization, and of programs of international co-operation, such as the Colombo plan. His anti-communism has not consisted of reckless denunciation, but of constructive efforts to prevent war and to help remove the social and economic grievances on which communism is nourished.
The editorial goes on to say:
With the exception of the most shortsighted nationalists, his program and personality have made him justly popular and respected in Canada and the United States. His record needs no defence.
Then further on:
The dangers inherent in the methods of the witch hunters cannot be overemphasized. A Mr. Victor Lasky, co-author of a book on the Alger Hiss case, has told a committee of the women's national Republican club that Mr. Pearson "consistently sabotaged" efforts to disclose Soviet intrigue in Washington and Ottawa. By inference, Mr. Lasky tried to raise doubts about Mr. Pearson's loyalty.
The method is by now well tried in the U.S. The America Firsters evidently find that they can intimidate opponents by raising the cry of disloyalty, or of "bad security risk", which has come to mean almost anyone who dissents from the lunatic fringe of the Republican party. With so many ex-communists as their chief source of information, it is hardly surprising that these people should use communist tactics-the smear, the implied guilt by association, the inference of disloyalty-against patriotic citizens who happen to be independent-minded.
The Toronto Daily Star on the same date says this:
Diplomatic quarters are aware that a campaign has been under way for about a year now to smear Mr. Pearson and to weaken Canada's voice in international affairs by the "lunatic fringe" of the U.S. Republican party.
The Toronto Globe and Mail, in a Saturday editorial, November 21, 1953, says:
The furore about Mr. Igor Gouzenko is deplorable. Washington is wrong in this argument, as probably the state department itself knows. But besides being wrong it is also being unfriendly. There is a suspicion, well founded, that the whole episode springs from a desire on the part of the McCarthyites to smear the Canadian government, External Affairs Minister Pearson in particular, and that the state department is aiding them because it is afraid of them.
The Ottawa Journal on November 20, 1953, in an editorial entitled "Beneath Contempt", says:
. . . Canadians have a right to ask that, throwing mud, American politicians throw it at themselves; do not try to pull down Canadian public men in the ugly process of pulling down their own.
Mr. Pearson was right in dismissing Lasky's talk as "beneath contempt". The trouble, however, is that some people don't know what is beneath contempt, and it must seem to many that the U.S. administration might and could do something to instruct its wild men in elementary manners towards their neighbours.
Now, by trying to smear the minister they hope to blackmail this government into handing over for their purposes and for their use 
Igor Gouzenko, who is a ward of the government, in order that he may provide for them another act in their variety show. As things stand now they have pretty well used up all their ammunition but they figure that Gouzenko will keep them on the front page for at least another month. To accomplish that, they have not hesitated to smear a distinguished member of this house and of the Canadian government.
I find it rather amusing that suddenly a great clamour has come from the various cat's-paws of McCarthyism for the production of Gouzenko in order that he may be used as new exhibit No. 1. I am quite sure that until a few days ago not one of them had ever heard his name or known of his existence. Now, all of a sudden, they have become authorities on the subject. They know all about Gouzenko and the valuable information they suggest he is so eager to give. What they are trying to do is to use a little blackmail on the government.
Before we lose sight of Gouzenko-and we should lose sight of him for everybody's good, including his own-let us remember one or two important things. On November 17, 1953, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), speaking on the orders of the day, made two things abundantly clear. The first thing was that Gouzenko himself said he had no information other than that reported in the royal commission on June 27, 1946, which is available to everyone for one dollar-and I am sure that the congressional committee can afford it. The second thing was that any information which could have been of value to the United States authorities or to any of our allies had originally been forwarded to them as soon as it became available. It is important to note that the whole transcript of his evidence, not what appeared in the report of the royal commission but a full transcript of his evidence, was sent to the United States government and other governments if they were concerned. I think that this house should recall that for the last seven years Mr. Gouzenko has not been in contact with spies. His bosom friends have been the R.C.M.P., and they have been good friends.
The McCarthyites now want Igor Gouzenko to join the circus and do some one-night stands on television. Their audiences have tired of the Bentleys and the Chamberses. The record of their parroting is more than slightly worn; in fact the record is downright cracked. Gouzenko is manna from Heaven to them.
When the publicity agencies and the public relations build-up boys hired by these various

congressional committees finish with Gouzenko and present him to the United States public, it will be hard for us to recognize him. He will not recognize himself. Nor will we be able to recognize the evidence that he gave before the royal commission.
Consider for a moment the build-up they can give him and will. Think of his name and his background. How well he fits into the script and what a great scenario they can write. Igor Gouzenko-a name that rings as Russian as Donald McDonald is Scotch; a cipher and code clerk with the air of mystery it implies. Ciphers and codes have always intrigued most people. Few know that one learns to do ciphers and codes as one does plumbing. Plumbing is more interesting and pays better, take my word for it. There is the incident of his visit to -the then prime minister's office, his being turned away, his unwelcome visits to other government offices, his return to his apartment, the Russian "goon" squad swooping down on him, his taking refuge in another apartment, protected by the Ottawa police department, and finally being rescued by the mounties and guarded by them for seven years.
This is the red meat for the build-up boys. The fact that he has no evidence is of no consequence. They are not interested in evidence or they would have read the report of the evidence that was sent to them. But the circus must go on. There you have it- intrigue, mystery, drama, action-and preserved by the mounties for McCarthy and Jenner and Velde. He brings them just what they need, namely a new face, a new name, a new angle, a new story and above all, what they love above everything else, headlines and more headlines. Before that congressional committee finishes with him they will build him up in the minds of a portion of the American people so that many of them will believe that he not only played the fiddle for the Czar but decoded Joe Stalin's most secret documents. You may ask, What about the evidence? It is not important for the committee's purpose, because the McCarthys, the Jenners, and the Veldes are not concerned in collecting evidence. Like dictators and tyrants everywhere at all times, they thrive on the spectacular, on providing a series of sensations, on constantly buttressing their position as defenders of freedom. So when the McCarthyites find that they have exhausted their propaganda, when they have squeezed dry the Whittaker Chamberses, the Elizabeth Bentleys and the other sudden
The Address-Mr. Croll converts, they find that they need a new script, a new scenario, and Igor Gouzenko fills that bill exactly.
To maintain their hold on public attention they must feed the press and the world at large some new meat to sate the appetite. The old records of prejudice and hate, the old tunes of guilt by association, of nonconformity, of red-tinged liberalism, were scratchy from constant playing. There had to be a new record, a hot rendition of the old tune but with a different metre. So they are satisfied to take a warmed-over Gouzenko. In their desperation to keep alive the flame of prejudice, they attempted to force ex-President Truman to testify. That attempt failed. They then booked Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation chief, and he was a half-day stand. It would appear that Mr. Hoover's defence will be that he really did not infringe on diplomatic courtesies and niceties because he only produced one copy of the top secret document that was alleged to have been sent by this government. In the light of that disclosure alone, how can anyone possibly consider producing Gouzenko under any circumstances if we wish to preserve national security?
What is important is that now for the first time we have a deliberate attempt to export McCarthyism to Canada. I am glad to say that up until now that vicious ideology has not been able to gain a foothold in this country. The big lie and the big smear have never had a place in Canadian politics; and, as the saying goes, we aim to keep it that way. But these purveyors of fear and hate overlooked the fact that a boundary line divides North America into two sovereign countries, and I repeat the expression "sovereign countries". When the United States state department-and I am sure with considerable reluctance-asked that the congressional committee be permitted, to question Gouzenko, the request was turned down for a good reason. The last thing we in this country want is to get ourselves involved in an American political hassle, for that is what it essentially is.
The rejection filled the McCarthyites with uncontrollable rage. How dare anyone have the temerity to say no to them? The New York Times, a very reliable paper, says that pressure is being exerted by the state department on the Canadian government to give ground. In order to attain their purpose, they have turned their guns on the minister, secure in the knowledge that he could not reply. The haters of the United Nations, in which the Secretary of State for

The Address-Mr. Croll External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is a distinguished figure, threw in their contribution to this attack. It was an opportunity to get in some whacks at a man who has done more for world peace in the forums of the United Nations than has any other single individual, because he refused to climb on the hate-wagon and by so doing weaken the very foundation of the democratic structure.
A second request for Igor Gouzenko has been made by Washington. This reveals the power of McCarthyism in the American political life, for a request is usually not renewed once it has been declined. In their eyes the sin of the minister is that he has retained his sanity and has not joined in the hymn of hate. He knows that if we do not defend the rights of others, we endanger our own. He has never hesitated to attack communist *aggression in and out of the United Nations; but his condemnation has been couched in temperate language, without the vicious extremes so often found in the speeches of those who profess to represent the American people. They fail to understand that one can hold strong views against communism without being intolerant.
No better friend of the United States, no greater supporter of our western democracy, and no more implacable foe of Russian communism can be found than Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs. Yet today we see a fantastic situation in which some power-drunk men in the United States are attempting to undermine him there and, I suppose they think, in this country. The very fact that it was necessary to reply-and it was-to the smear campaign now in progress is a grim reminder to this house and to this country that fear can become an instrument of policy in the hands of unscrupulous men. No one is more worthy of public confidence, both in Canada and in the United States, than is Lester B. Pearson. Yet today we find powerful political elements in the United States attempting to picture him and Canada as pink-hued left-wingers with a soft spot for communism. He has the antagonism of some people who rely upon judgment by attack and the weight of insults to win their case. Because he does not join the pack when it appears popular and like a wolf tear the prey to pieces, he is in turn attacked by the pack.
The Russians do not like the minister, and with good reason. He represents a substantial stumbling-block to communist aspirations because logic and reason are his weapons, and he cannot be stampeded into doing what the Soviets would like him to do.

Whatever Mr. Lasky may think, it is very clear that the Kremlin does not consider Mr. Pearson to be a Soviet tool. Twice in 1946 and again in 1952, the Russians vetoed Mr. Pearson in regard to the critical post of Secretary General of the United Nations. Pravda, the official organ of the communist party, made a vicious personal attack, claiming that Mr. Pearson was:
. . . designated by officials for this high post because of his devotion to American moneybags . . .
-and his "zealousness toward the American military". Pravda went on to state categorically that Mr. Pearson was an American agent.
This spring Pravda developed a new theme. On February 4 the official Moscow newspaper carried an article suggesting that Mr. Pearson's real motive was to bring about the absorption of Canada by the United States. Among other things, Pravda stated:
As regards the reasons for the special effort of Pearson himself to carry through to the end the enslavement of the Canadian people by the American monopolies, these reasons are generally known. Pearson began his career in one of the leading American concerns for the production. of weapons, Armour and Company, and is up till now a participant in this enterprise. Pearson also possesses a considerable quantity of stock of the largest Canadian metal concern, International Nickel Company of Canada, in which the decisive role belongs to American capital. It is not difficult to understand where people like Pearson, nicknamed by the people "American Minister in Canada", are leading Canada.
I think the time has come to serve a "hands off" notice to McCarthyism. The time has come for us to let them know that we are not going to bend our knee to political blackmail. The time has come to bring home to them we are not going to be pushed around.
The lunatic fringe in the United States has been gunning for the Secretary of State for External Affairs for some time. Because he will not play their game in the United Nations, he has been accused of being soft to communism. Now they have delivered their first Sunday punch. Do as we say or we will smear you. Well, maybe the smear works south of the border but it will not work in Canada. This time the McCarthyites have picked the wrong country and the wrong man for their smear campaign.
Our record on subversives is an open book. We cleared them out in 1946, long before the world ever heard of McCarthy, Jenner and Velde, and we did it in the normal Canadian fashion and preserved fundamental rights. We did not need a congressional committee and television to help us clean house. The royal commission was empowered by order in council dated February 5, 1946.
It investigated and made its final report on

June 27, 1946. As is well known, prosecutions were then launched and the guilty parties brought to justice.
What is more, the Canadian government passed along full information to the United States authorities at that time. If they did not take the trouble to read it, it is not too late now. We did not hide anything in a pumpkin. Now, seven years later, the McCarthyites and the pumpkin heads have the effrontery to come to us and accuse us of being soft to communism. They want to drag us into the act, to blame us, and make us the whipping-boy. If we refuse to let Gouzenko perform then they are prepared to set up Canada, and particularly the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as their next candidate for trial by slander.
If McCarthyism achieves complete dominance over American political thinking, if it succeeds in strangling liberalism in the United States, if it achieves a dim-out of freedom, then Russia and communism will have achieved a great victory without striking a blow. We Canadians want no part of American political warfare. We can only regret this dismemberment of freedom, but it is their business, not ours. We speak of the American way of life. Now we can speak of the American way of politics. We belong to the British tradition and we want Americans to know that, if they do not.
What is going on in the United States at the present time is not a pretty picture. We cannot subscribe to it. To us it is unthinkable. If that is the American way in politics that is their business and their problem, but it must not be exported to us.
I think the time has come for the government to take an even more positive position in this matter and to re-emphasize to our good neighbours and to the world a few simple truths. We are against communism without any buts or ifs, and we are against subversives without the slightest qualification. We are ready and willing to cooperate with every free country in the world to oppose communism and to stamp out subversion wherever it may appear. We are ready to do these things and more to the limit of our ability, freely and willingly, and we have demonstrated it time and time again. But we will not be intimidated by the big lie and the big smear. We believe that the best defence to communism is still more democracy. We will not resist communism by embracing McCarthyism.	We
want no part of either of them. As for us, a plague on both their houses.
Now, I just have one last word. The President of the United States spoke up when McCarthyism attacked the former president of the United States. The Secretary of State
The Address-Mr. Montgomery for External Affairs is equally well known to the President of the United States and he knows that the minister commands the esteem and confidence of the Canadian people. By the same token we want consideration from our American friends. The attacks on a member of the Canadian government are shocking and should be repudiated by no less a person than the President of the United States.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I should like to convey congratulations, through you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, to the Speaker upon his recent election to the high office of Speaker of this assembly. I am a fairly new member with very little experience in parliament but in that short time I can say from my experience that I am sure that all members will be treated fairly and justly by the Speaker, that he will bring to his high office great dignity and that we will be proud of him as our Speaker. To you also, sir, I wish to convey my congratulations on your choice as Deputy Speaker. I should also like to join with other hon. members in extending congratulations to the mover (Mr. Holling-worth) and the seconder (Mr. Villeneuve) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I represent a rural constituency where the majority of the people are engaged in agriculture and lumbering, and the chief agricultural product in my constituency being potatoes it will be readily understood that the marketing price of potatoes has a lot to do with the economy and social life of my people. During the debate so far I have listened with a great deal of interest to speeches concerning the problems of the western farmers which appear to revolve around wheat. I am naturally interested, as wheat and other grains grown in such large quantities affect the whole economy of Canada, but in western Canada, farming is on such a gigantic scale compared with the small owners in the east that I suppose for that reason the western farmer gets more attention. In fact, we from the maritimes often feel that he receives too much consideration. However, in listening to these reports I was glad to learn that they have enjoyed at least three good years, although it would seem that the three good crops were more or less a blessing in disguise. But, Mr. Western Farmer, even with all your difficulties I doubt if you have as many worries as our farmers in the east and in particular the potato growers. Potatoes are a very necessary food, but a crop which cannot be carried over. They must be marketed within ten months of their harvest or they are a total loss. Potatoes are also
242	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Montgomery an expensive crop to grow because expensive machinery is needed for planting and harvesting. In addition, expensive fertilizers must be used at planting time and spraying must be continued more or less throughout the summer. The cost of production runs from about $1.75 to $2 per barrel, which is 165 pounds. The determination of that cost depends upon the yield, of course. This means that the producer must get an average of $2 per barrel or approximately 80 cents per bushel to break even. Add to this the cost of storage, bags, handling and shipping, and it is readily seen that potatoes must retail at approximately three cents per pound in order for the grower to break even. When any hon. member is able to buy potatoes for less than three cents per pound, he may be sure that there are many farmers in my province who are working long hours for practically nothing.
Some hon. members may believe this sounds fantastic, nevertheless it is a fact. A recent report to me indicates that potatoes are selling today at 65 cents a barrel at the farm, and they are not moving very fast. This barrel of potatoes is costing the farmer, on an average, $2 to produce.
Occasionally, but not often, there is a scarcity of potatoes such as was experienced in the spring of 1952. Potato prices were high, and those farmers who had storage space and were able to keep their potatoes for the first few months came out of that crop year very well. Some of them made money. However, the 1952 crop was just the opposite, and it may be a surprise to many hon. members to learn that potatoes were dumped. This year the crop is average and the quality is good. Disposal of this crop is essential to our economy. We are by no means as fortunate as the western farmer, because our crop cannot be carried over from year to year, and this is the second consecutive difficult year. Out of the proceeds of this crop, not only the farmers but the merchants and others expect to get their accounts cleaned up. This is the period of the year when the rural municipalities expect to get their taxes collected; the banks expect their loans to be repaid; and children are talking about Santa Claus.
The potato farmer in my province is bedevilled by the high cost of production, unfair competition from the United States producers, high freight rates and dull markets, so he certainly needs courage. He is faced with the tax collector, the machinery agent, the sheriff, and most pathetic of all, if he is a family man, a lean Christmas. In my constituency there are three starch factories


and a potato chip factory. These are private enterprise industries which have been a boon to the potato producer- in some seasons. They handle a lot of potatoes, but the price that they can pay depends upon the price that they can get for their products. The prospects for starch this year are not very bright.
Groups of farmers and shippers have recently formed a marketing board whose representatives, together with experts from the department of agriculture, are working with officials from the federal Department of Agriculture under the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act. We are hoping that a sound and acceptable solution will be worked out so that some stability may be given to the marketing of this staple product. Certainly, we are all looking forward to an improvement when this board starts functioning because, in theory, it seems to be approaching the matter from the proper standpoint.
I should like to mention the matter of unfair competition from the United States producer to which I referred a moment ago. He is allowed to market his crop in Canada free of duty, with the exception of six weeks in midsummer. On behalf of the eastern potato grower I would ask the government to keep that fact in mind when trade problems are being discussed with our friends to the south or when present treaties are being considered for renewal. There is, however, a bright spot for some of the farmers who, as a a result of being forced out of the potato business, turned to the raising of grain. Last year quite a few farmers confined their planting to oats, and they are quite fortunate because there has been a good market for this product. In common with apples, oats are bringing a very good price. However, there is not a large amount of oats produced in New Brunswick, and in my constituency the amount of apples grown is extremely small.
I should like to mention another industry in our province, and that is our forest products industry. Our province depends upon lumber and pulp for a large part of its income. In 1952 the products of the pulp and paper industry amounted to around $100 million. The products of the small mills accounted for $20 million, and other wood products accounted for about $30 million, making in all a total of $150 million from our forest products. The matter of the preservation of our forests is of grave concern to us. The war against the spruce budworm alone is costing the province of New Brunswick more than $1 million annually, and in addition large sums must be spent for fire protection. So far as I know, no other province

in Canada is so concerned about the protection oi its forests, and I doubt if the forests *of any other province contribute so much to the economic and social life of its people. We are dependent to a tremendous degree upon the income from this source.
For the reasons I have stated, it is important to mention forest products here because it is important that markets be maintained. It is vital that every assistance be given to obtaining markets. This fact was brought to my attention forcibly by a number of small mill owners just before I left home. I find that many of these mill owners still have last year's cut on their hands, so they are in doubt as to whether operations should be carried out next year. Some of these small operators cannot afford to pay for woods crews, and this of course causes hardship to those people who are dependent upon these woods operations for their income.
The other day the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) gave you a very vivid picture of the fishing industry, which is not bright, and the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick) talked of conditions in Newfoundland. It is pretty much the same pattern all over the maritimes. Apparently we overproduce: or Is it, if you want to put it that way, a lack of proper distribution? In any case we need markets. Our producers are not sharing fairly in the distribution of the wealth of this country. Therefore, I join with those hon. members in asking the government to give every assistance and cooperation to these industries in securing markets that will keep them in a sound position.
I have mentioned conditions generally, Mr. Speaker, from which I trust you can see that we also in New Brunswick have serious problems; but with co-operation from the government I believe-at least I hope-our economic position can be improved.
My province is one of the smaller ones, and the economy has expanded at a much slower rate than the general economy of Canada as a whole. For instance, since 1946- that is since the end of the second world war-the personal incomes of the people of New Brunswick have not increased more than 25 per cent, while the general average increase in Canada as a whole has been approximately 38 per cent.
We have many small industries in New Brunswick that are worthy of mention, that are meeting national and international competition, and which contribute greatly to the stability of our economy. I now come to what we hope will be one of the brightest spots in the development of our province, namely
The Address-Mr. Montgomery the mineral resources. Within the last eighteen months it has been discovered that we possess a very great natural resource which has untold possibilities, namely large base metal deposits of high value. If my information is correct, New Brunswick may have some of the greatest base metal ore bodies on this North American continent, some of which are now being prepared for milling early next summer, with prospects of far greater developments to follow.
I am told that some 40,000 claims have already been staked in the Gloucester and nearby districts known as the Bathurst area, and there are hundreds more all over the province. In fact some very encouraging prospects have been located in my own constituency. As far as I can find out, I do not believe these prospects are based upon a wave of wild speculation, because many of the larger and more conservative mining interests in North America are taking an active interest in the New Brunswick mining situation. Millions of dollars have already been spent and will be spent during the next year in drilling, surveys and other forms of investigation. This new discovery of our mineral potential gives us hope. Already the people of some parts of our province are enthusiastic and full of enterprise.
But with these new hopes and possibilities also come problems. Possibly one of the most urgent is the supply of power. It has been generally recognized that New Brunswick's slower progress has been due to the lack of power development. We are not so fortunate as many other provinces, in that we do not have many large power possibilities. However, we do have one source of approved possible development. I refer to the Saint John river basin. The full and final development is going to entail agreements with the state of Maine and Quebec, which comprise part of the basin and where important storage facilities are necessary, which we all hope will in due course be worked out to the satisfaction of all parties concerned.
What I wish to point out and what I wish to confine my remarks to now is what we call the first phase or river flow development, which is so important to us in the immediate future for the development of our mineral area and to meet the natural annual increased demand and also the new load which may be required for our new military camp, which is also a new and important development.
I refer to the Beechwood site on the Saint John river. It is located in my constituency. It has been surveyed and approved and I am informed recommended for immediate development in so far as the first phase or run of
244	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Montgomery river basis is concerned, which does not involve any outside interests. The initial installation at this site will bring into production two 45,000 horsepower units, with an estimated annual output of approximately 355 million kilowatt hours. Another important consideration is the cost of the power delivered to the industry. Thus the cost of development will have a bearing on the cost of power. From information I have been able to obtain, the cost of the Beechwood development and the necessary power lines will exceed $45 million.
This of course is going to be a very heavy burden on a small province like New Brunswick. We already have a heavy burden of debt in proportion to our present ability to pay. Our interest rates are high. But confronting us is a great opportunity, if we can find the money at a rate of interest which will permit the power development at a price which is attractive enough for the smelters and subsidiary industries to utilize our resources to the fullest extent.
I am reminded of the boy who was looking at a luscious apple on a tree. He wanted it so badly, but it was just beyond his reach. He could not get it until a man came along and gave him a little lift. Then he obtained the apple. The people of New Brunswick are in that position: a golden opportunity is waiting in the full development of our base metal resources, provided we furnish the power at a reasonable cost, which may very well be the turning point for prosperity for the future.
I believe other provinces have an interest in the prosperity of New Brunswick. In fact I am sure prosperity spreads, and we are all interested in one another. That being true, the problems and prosperity of one part must be responsibilities or assets of the dominion as a whole. Thus this government is justified in going to the aid of any province to assist in the development of natural resources which are helpful and beneficial to the economy of the whole nation, if that province is unable to carry the development itself in the early stages.
I should like to read from a report of a conference of the premiers of the Atlantic provinces held last September, in which appears a statement made by Premier Flemming which I think is very timely when discussing this subject. I quote:
It has been said that no nation can exist "half slave and half free"-that was said of the United States before the civil war. Well-in Canada-it seems to me that we cannot exist with have and have-not provinces-cannot exist partly prosperous and partly depressed. Such conditions of economic injustice and unbalance will always be threats to national unity and to that integration of aim and purpose essential to the development of full nationhood.


I think it can be fairly said that New Brunswick has been one of the have-not provinces, and it is generally agreed that the retarded state of its economy has been due to a lack of cheap electrical power. This fact was emphasized by the report of the New Brunswick committee on reconstruction published in 1944. It was one of the chief reasons New Brunswick did not get extensive contracts for production of war materials during the second world war, when this country as a whole was expanding rapidly in the industrial field.
If the need for cheap hydroelectric power was urgent in 1944 it is much more urgent today, with the great mineral resources awaiting development. Whereas the installed capacity of hydroelectric power is more than one horsepower per capita of the population in Canada, in New Brunswick it is only one-quarter horsepower per capita of its population.
Therefore it should be abundantly clear that the development of cheap hydroelectric power in my province is the key to unlock the treasure which promises to revolutionize the economy of New Brunswick. That will put in balance conditions that will remove the apparent economic injustices that have in the past threatened our national unity.
Hon. members may be wondering why New Brunswick has not developed more of her available resources. That is a fair question and I will try to give a fair answer. As I have already said, we have been a province of have-nots; we have heavy debts in proportion to the ability of our people to pay. We must look to outsiders to purchase our securities and, unfortunately, interest rates are high. During the next few years, if power is to be made available, our indebtedness is bound to increase tremendously, during which period we cannot expect adequate returns. Therefore interest rates on the money required to develop the power will be a major factor in determining the price of power to industry.
The price must be reasonably attractive to be of value. With the new discoveries of the vast and valuable mineral resources, I believe New Brunswick is a good risk for investment. The power development is a must. I sincerely believe it is the foundation of a new progressive economy that will provide prosperity for our people. It will provide work and markets at home. It will provide greater income for our people and larger revenues for the dominion.
Involved in the development of the Beech-wood site on the Saint John river, and other

sites-Beechwood is not the only one, but it has already been approved and that is why I refer to it-is the all-important question of water conservation, a matter in which I am glad to say this government has shown considerable interest. I do not intend to speak further on conservation at this time as that matter can be dealt with at a later date, but in the few minutes left I should like to summarize what I have endeavoured to say.
The prosperity of our agricultural industry in New Brunswick seems to be stalled due to high costs of production, international competition, high freight rates and distant markets which cause too great a spread between the producer's market and the consumer's market, a retarded economy due to the lack of developed hydroelectric power, and a debt structure which demands a high rate of interest, which is a handicap to the securing of capital for the development of cheap power.
A golden opportunity now presents itself in the discovery of great base metal resources, equal to any on the North American continent. However, there is an urgent need of cheap power for the development of said resources and the encouragement of new industry. Cheap money is needed to develop the required power.
I have tried in my rambling remarks to place before this house and the government some of the difficult problems of my province-others were brought to your attention by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart)-all of which can and will, I hope, be supported by other hon. members from our province.
I am not asking for handouts, I am not speaking on behalf of any party or government, but I am speaking for the people of my constituency, yes and for the people generally in New Brunswick. Like the boy who needed the lift to get the apple, the people of New Brunswick need a lift. We need the co-operation and good will of other provinces and the people generally, as well as of this government. I believe New Brunswick is on the threshold of a great future. Development of power is the key to prosperity. With recent discoveries of vast mineral resources we have become a good risk for investment.
If it becomes necessary for New Brunswick to seek assistance from this government in the development of power, I hope and trust a way will be found for giving that assistance and co-operation to permit cheap power development to become a reality on our interprovincial and international Saint John
The Address

Mr. Hahn river, in conjunction with a great and important conservation project. Personally, it seems to me, it would be sound government policy to assist any province in the development of natural resources which will lift that province out of a retarded and stagnant economy to become a prosperous and thriving member of the family of provinces within the dominion.
Just before I sit down I should like to refer to two other matters, the first being veterans and veterans affairs. I have always strongly supported, although not at great length, legislation for the veterans. I hope a veterans affairs committee will be set up at this session, and that the requests made by the Canadian Legion on behalf of the veterans will be considered most seriously. One thing in particular I should like to see is the elimination of the ceiling on the income a veteran may earn and still receive his veterans allowance.
I should like to say a word about possible legislation concerning the blind. I submit that legislation should be brought forward to give more consideration to the blind. I would want to see this legislation before discussing it more fully, but I do want to say that there are many blind or nearly blind persons today who are enduring hardships because they are not in receipt of blind pensions. Apparently they cannot get the pension when they have certain property or income, and I think that stipulation should be revised or possibly eliminated.

speechtext:
Mr. Deputy Speaker, I should like to convey through you my best wishes to Mr. Speaker upon his elevation to the high office he now holds. I should like also to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) and the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Villeneuve) upon the fine way in which they went about moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I am not here to apologize on behalf of the people of British Columbia for the fact that they have elected a Social Credit government. They did so of their own volition. It was their democratic right to do so and, having done so, we accept it as our duty to give them the best type of government we can. We hope that within the next few years we will be able to announce that there is a second debt-free province in this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Possibly those of our provinces which are having difficulty in this day and age might take a lesson from the far west.

The Address-Mr. Hahn

speechtext:
I would beg the indulgence of the house while I tell you something about our province and, more particularly, the riding which I represent.
The city of New Westminster, which has a population of about 28,000, is fortunate indeed that it has so many versatile athletes. This year it has two dominion championships to its credit, namely the dominion soccer champions, the New Westminster Royals, as they are called, and the junior lacrosse champions of Canada, the New Westminster Salmonacs.
Outside the city proper we have four divisions:	Surrey municipal district, the
largest municipality in the British Empire, the municipality of Delta and the municipality of Langley. We generally divide Surrey into two regions, North Surrey and South Surrey. That gives the four divisions I mentioned.
Surrey municipality, this particularly large region, has a voting population of about 28,000. Add to that the population of New Westminster and you have the second largest electoral district in point of population west of the city of Toronto. We have approximately
53.000	electors in the area and naturally, because of its great expansion, we have a number of industries in the area. We have heavy industry in the lumber mills with their very large payrolls. The other industries in the city are largely fishing, box making and smaller industries which go along with the lumbering industry.
The population of the city has long overflowed the boundaries and today we find sections of North Surrey very heavily populated, especially in the Whalley, Bridgeview, and South Westminster areas. With the heavy influx of people we have need of more and more housing, and we are particularly happy to see that the speech from the throne indicates the possibility of getting more housing in our area.
Naturally enough, the fine city of New Westminster requires a thriving hinterland. In the municipality of Langley we find dairying and small fruit farming extensively practised. In Surrey we have intensive vegetable market gardening, poultry raising, dairying and summer trade. We are fortunate in having the only summer resort on the Pacific coast lower mainland, the hamlet of White Rock, which has a population of between
7.000	and 8,000. In Delta we have dairying and potato production.
This is just an outline, sir, of the area.
[Mr. Hahn.l
I was particularly interested to hear the various addresses that have been made in the past several days. The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy) told us that things had never been better. As the days have gone by it seems to me that we have heard nothing but crying of woe and of more woe. We seem to have a fishing problem, a wheat problem, a potato problem, an English car problem and even a Gouzenko problem; and today I read that we have an overproduction of parliamentarians, which gives us another problem.
One of the specific problems of my area with which I wish to deal was dealt with also by the hon. member for Westmorland. That is the fishing problem. He said things had never been better, but I noticed that he did have the problem of fish. I have that problem in my area too; but before I deal with it specifically, sir, I would like to congratulate some of the men who have taken such an active part in the work of the international commission for the protection of sockeye salmon. They did a marvellous job. One is Senator Tom Reid, from my own area. Another who had a great deal to do with the committee was John Babcock, and in this connection I read from an editorial in the Vancouver Province of November 17, 1953:
Years ago, John Babcock, deputy minister of fisheries at Victoria, used to make speeches urging measures to restore and conserve the salmon fisheries of the Fraser. With proper measures, he insisted, the annual fish crop from the Fraser could be built up to a value of $30,000,000 ... In the end, it produced the international salmon commission, which, after years of investigation, evolved plans for the restoration of the Fraser's glories . . .
The $30,000,000 target has not been hit yet. But an encouraging start has been made. The efforts of the commission are beginning to prove themselves.
This same salmon problem may be divided into two parts. First, we have a lack of markets. We are told that there is an overproduction of fish. Second, and an even more acute problem, we are not allowed to catch the fish. In the British Columbian of November 10, we find the following:
The Fraser fishing area-the only one still left open in B.C.-will be restricted to Monday and Tuesday each week until further notice. From Wednesday, November 11, to the following Monday, the river will be closed to allow escapement of salmon to the spawning areas.
Reasons for the drastic step in curtailment of river fishing-a further blow to local fishermen who have already had to contend with a light run of chum salmon-were given by the fisheries department as poor escapement, a light run, increased fishing efficiency and the influx of large numbers of "outsiders" who have come to the Fraser now the other grounds have been closed.
The closing of the Fraser is a very, very important thing in the lives of the fishermen.

We have a large fishing population along the Fraser river, and each one of those fishermen has an investment of anywhere up to $10,000 in gill-net boats with which they usually catch salmon. Now they are told they cannot catch fish and the reason given is that "outsiders" are catching the pink salmon. As we have an international sockeye commission I would suggest that its powers be extended to cover the commencement of research on the problem of conserving the salmon fishing in order to make it possible for the gill netters to go on fishing pink salmon. I am requesting that extension of powers in order to get a sufficient number of fishermen out on the Fraser again.
The "outsiders" happen to come from the state of California, I am told. They come with their large boats, having done their fishing to the south, into the mouth of the Juan de Fuca, and catch the fish before they come into the Fraser channel. We have to conserve them from there on in. It is not a good deal; and, as fisheries in the United States are under the jurisdiction of the state, I am sure the federal government and. the state of Washington could arrive at a regulation that would be binding upon both.
Next, sir, is this matter of markets. In this instance I have here from the Financial Post a feature article dated November 20 in which we read this:
Probably more than any other industry in British Columbia, fishing has been the victim of overseas sales slump. Before the war British Columbia canned salmon was being marketed in 40 different countries. Today only about half a dozen countries regularly buy from this province, and that includes the Canadian domestic market and the United States, never much of a market for canned salmon because of the tariff.
Last year, Britain bought no canned salmon here at all although it used to be the mainstay of the industry and during the war bought nearly the entire British Columbia pack in two or three years. This year, Britain bought sparingly. The industry hopes that because of the economic improvement in Britain this year, sales will be much larger in 1954, but no firm commitments have been made.
Then, sir, I should like the government particularly to note this:
A delegation of leading British Columbia packers recently returned from a series of conferences in England. The purpose of their mission was to sell canned salmon. But in order to get even a favourable consideration they had to give assurance that the fishing industry in British Columbia would make an effort to make the necessary dollars available through purchase of more British engines, nets and other gear.
How unfortunate it is, sir, that though this little band of men in this section of the house begged the government not to sign the Bretton Woods agreement, they did so. Otherwise we might have sold our fish, at least to Britain.
The Address-Mr. Hahn
I am always ready to help someone who is ready to help himself. We find that this is what has happened. In the Vancouver Province of November 16 we read:
The British Columbia fishing industry has made its first move to attempt balancing trade between this province and United Kingdom by ordering a 34-foot vessel from a Scottish shipyard.
A delegation from the industry, headed by J. M. Buchanan, president of B.C. Packers, has completed a two-month trade tour of the U.K. in an effort to increase purchases of British goods . . .
A spokesman for the industry here said no attempt was made to secure further orders for B.C. canned salmon.
"This purchase is simply designed to show our willingness to do business", he said.
B.C. fishermen already buy most of their linen nets from the U.K.
That is very true, sir. British Columbia fishermen do buy most of their nets from the United Kingdom. They are trying their best to find a market for their fish.
One of the earlier speakers today said the fishermen were not wealthy enough to go to Britain to find their own markets. It makes it rather difficult when a small industry has to send its own trade envoys to the other nations of the world in order to get markets for its goods. Certainly there should be a way whereby our surplus could be got rid of without small trade delegations being sent to every nation in the world by these small companies or fishermen.
Another immediate problem that I find in my province is this one of lumbering. Up to the present time lumbering has been one of the staple industries in the province. That industry again is dependent on the home market. That home market today is lacking. It is lacking more particularly because farmers on the prairies have not been able to sell their wheat. So if we can advance 75 cents a bushel to start this economy rolling again it might be of some value to the people of British Columbia, more particularly the lumber operators. The slashing of lumber production is very definite. There are no ifs, ands or buts about it. In the British Columbian of November 13 we find an article headed "Plywood Output Slashed" in which it is stated:
MacMillan and Bloedel Ltd., announced the layoff in its Vancouver and Port Alberni plywood mills. It said curtailed production of fir plywood was necessitated bv the first drop-off in twenty years in an annually-increasing Canadian demand for plywood.
The company said crews would be called back to work as soon as market conditions improved, possibly early next year.
I do not know where the newspaper gets its information to the effect that the market will improve next year, unless some governmental official may have passed along the
248	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Hahn word that next year the government was going to advance 75 cents a bushel to the farmers so they could go ahead and buy the goods they required.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think we should be too complacent in our thoughts with regard to this matter of trade. It is very important. We can see how, more particularly, the production of wheat and the buying of this wheat by the government has a very important effect upon the economy of the country.
There is one further problem that I have to ask you to listen to, and that would be the problem of agriculture as it applies to my particular area. In Washington, D.C., on April 3, 1953, Secretary of Agriculture Ezra Taft Benson issued the following warning:
A crop of 3S5 million bushels is 25 to 30 million bushels more than is needed to meet fully all national requirements for potatoes. Such excess production will cut two ways-per bushel prices will be reduced to farmers more than proportionately since the total crop will be worth less and costs of operating the larger acreage would of course be increased.
Mr. Speaker, what Secretary of Agriculture Benson said is quite true. It has been proved that the Americans increased their crop to 395 million bushels, that there was an excess of 25 or 35 million bushels, and that we became the dumping market for it.
There is a very odd state of affairs in the province of British Columbia where vegetables are concerned, as well as potatoes; I include potatoes as a vegetable in this instance. As was mentioned by one of the former speakers, our vegetable crop usually comes two to three weeks later than that of the United States. The result is that the United States early potato, vegetable and fruit crops come into our part of the province and steal the cream of the market. They get the money and we get what is left.
In the case of the potato growers the problem is similar, but a rather awkward situation evolves. Most of the potatoes that come into British Columbia-that is, the very early potatoes-come from the state of California and the state of Washington. From the state of California to British Columbia the freight rate is about 34 cents a hundredweight less than it would be from California to Manitoba for those same potatoes. Hence this is what we find. California sends potatoes into British Columbia and British Columbia sends new potatoes to Manitoba. If California were to be encouraged, by some edict, to send their potatoes to Manitoba rather than to British Columbia, the potato growers of British Columbia would have no worry. But they have no market at home because the California growers happen to be marketing


the second early potatoes When our early potatoes come on, so we are left holding the bag.
Mr. Speaker, I would beg of this government to please take these things into consideration when formulating their policies. Our potato problem is apparently not the only one in the country. In his address a short while ago the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) dealt quite extensively with the potato problem as it exists in the province of New Brunswick. They have a marketing problem as well. It is true that from the point of view of acreage we probably do not have such an extensive crop as that of New Brunswick, but certainly we do have a similar problem on marketing, and it is the marketing problem that has to be taken care of.
