Mr. Speaker, I have delayed my participation in this debate because, as a new member, I felt it wise to give time and opportunity to more experienced members to point the way. But now that I can discern a pattern to which I can conform, I trust what I have to say may not be out of :place and may be considered a contribution to this debate.
Evidently it is usual, Mr. Speaker, for all hon. members first to offer congratulations to you on your election to the high office to which you have been called. While I associate myself with all the very pleasant things that have been said, might I vary the procedure somewhat by congratulating the members of this house on their good fortune in having chosen one whose evident skill and firmness in conducting the debates in this chamber is accompanied by a graciousness and charm which is the envy of us all.
The mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and the seconder (Mr. Villeneuve) of the address have already received their meed of praise, and I associate myself with that. I hope that I shall do as well. Many members from both sides of the house and from all parties have already spoken, and I note with satisfaction that at times there has been no lack of that vigour and forthrightness in presenting a point of view which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) described as that cut and thrust so necessary and desirable if right decisions are to be the outcome of our deliberations here.
We who are in public life, and particularly those of us who have given some time to the
study of the behaviour of man in his relations with his fellows, have learned, if we have learned anything at all, that we differ from one another in every conceivable way; and what -a blessing this is. How dull would

life be, Mr. Speaker, if each of us were a replica of his fellow; and how terrible it would be if we all looked alike, thought alike and believed alike. It is through our differences that we tolerate one another, and it is the recognition that there must be different points of view that brings us together in friendly association to hammer out on the anvil of free and open discussion those compromises which are the outcome of the parliamentary system.
The recognition of these very human traits, this coming together to reconcile differing points of view, this willingness to compromise by giving way a little here and gaining a little there, this belief that half a loaf is better than no loaf at all, this belief in all of us that a compromise solution is the best that can be achieved at that time and is a step toward complete agreement, are signs of maturity, the genius of our people, and the foundation of our democracy. I trust that in any part I may play in this house I may be given insight to see the good intent in all men.
It is with pride that I present myself as the choice of the electors of that constituency in British Columbia which has at its centre the capital city of Victoria. My constituency embraces also the municipality of Oak Bay to the north, and also the municipality of Esquimalt, which includes the naval dockyard and H.M.C.S. Naden. The official name of the constituency is Victoria. I notice that there are two other Victorias represented in the house, the others identifying themselves by carrying a subsidiary title. It is a matter of regret to me that representatives of the other Victorias are on the other side of the house.
I suppose there have been times when members from British Columbia have extolled the beauties and wealth of the province, and have extolled also the vigour and strength of its people. All they have said or could have said is true, but I shall resist the temptation to repeat it. I have been sobered by reading a description of us by that master of the very apt quip, Premier Douglas of Saskatchewan. In an address to the chamber of commerce in Regina not very long ago he is reported to have said:
Tile people of British Columbia look upon others with the pity of Adam and Eve looking at someone who wasn't born in the garden of Eden.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, we are quite as bad as that, but we do have a very natural pride in the accomplishments, the
The Address-Mr. Fairey beauties and the vigour of our own province. I intend to speak for a few minutes of British Columbia in a very general way, if my colleagues from that province will permit me to do so, in order to bring to the attention of the house and the government the handicaps occasioned by its geographical features which militate against its more rapid development. Its great need is more and better communications, not only within the province itself but with its sister provinces.
I would remind you, sir, that the province is riven by four great mountain ranges-the Rockies, the Selkirks, the Cascades and the coast range. All of these run in a general north and south direction and until recent years farmed a very effective barrier between us and the rest of Canada. Between these ranges are extensive and fertile valleys through which flow great and mighty rivers, offering almost unbounded opportunities for the development of great hydroelectric power systems. The opportunities for the exercise of personal initiative are recognized by people who accept the risks attendant upon pioneer adventure in the hope -and -expectation of rich reward.
That is why our province has attracted to it those from other provinces and other countries, those -adventurous souls who have made such a great contribution to our growth, unequalled a-nywhere in Canada.
When I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the population of British Columbia increased about 47 per cent in the last decade, -and compare it with the over-all increase of 22 per -cent for C-anada as a whole, it is to indicate how attractive -the opportunities have proved to be to so many people.
Much has been said during this debate about the problems -being faced by agriculture in the prairie provinces. These problems are real and -affect us all. Lack of cash on the prairies affects the sale of our lumber and lumber products, our salmon and our fruit; but because this matter has been dealt with effectively by -the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and because I have nothing new to contribute to what has already been said on that subject, I do not intend to pursue it further. Rather would I emphasize the growth of industry in this country, and the degree -to which decentralization of industry is taking -place. More and more is industry moving to British -Columbia, and mo-re and more is it found possible and desirable to establish secondary industries close to the source of -their raw materials.
Despite -the rapid growth already evident iu our province, it is my conviction that the
250	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fairey high cost of providing adequate communication systems delays a development which would be to the benefit of Canada as a whole. I am aware that the provision of roads, bridges and the like within a province is the sole concern of each provincial government. However, any large scheme of development and the opening up of rich lands to settlement such as are found in northern British Columbia is a task beyond the capacity of local government without federal assistance. The federal government has quite properly co-operated with the provinces, looking forward to the ultimate completion of the trans-Canada highway, by contributing 50 per cent of the cost of construction according to agreed upon standards.
I have been at some pains to describe the rugged terrain over which this trans-Canada highway must pass in British Columbia. May I emphasize now the problem facing a population boastfully placed at something less than a million and a half people. The average cost of constructing a road in British Columbia to trans-Canada standards, including black top, is $140,000 per mile. There are sections of the road, however, passing through the Fraser canyon which have cost nearly a million dollars per mile. As a matter of fact there are two sections between Yale and Lyitton, one of which is a mile long and the other four-tenths of a mile, and they cost just under $1 million per mile. The average cost of all roads in British Columbia is $140,000 per mile, but the average cost through Kicking Horse pass east of Golden and through the Fraser canyon is about $240,000 per mile.
X know it is a fact, and it is gratefully acknowledged, that the federal government pays half of that on the trans-Canada highway. I would point out, however, that the remaining half, which is borne by the people of the province, represents a sum in excess of the total cost of similar roads in other provinces. When we consider that the province is obliged to pay the total cost of all other roads throughout such a large and rugged province, and which are just as costly, it seems reasonable to urge that consideration should be given to the establishment of some differential in the proportion of grants to costs, particularly where excessive costs are encountered and where the roads are interprovincial in their scope and are intended to bind us more closely together as citizens of Canada.
While I am on the subject of communication, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word about my own constituency, which is on the largest of the many islands off the coast of British Columbia. Vancouver island is nearly


300 miles long. It contains immense tracts of the finest merchantable timber. In that timber there are stands of the finest and biggest fir and cedar trees in the province. Moreover, in the last three years we have seen established in the northern part of the island a number of plywood plants and pulp-wood mills costing millions of dollars. On the southern tip of this island stands the capital city of Victoria. On the west coast there are numerous fishing villages and processing plants connected with the fishing industry. Yet it is a fact that communication by sea between the mainland at Vancouver and the capital city of Victoria and other places on the island is less adequate than it has been for many years.
It is not enough to point out that aircraft are now available. You cannot transport goods in any quantity by air. Sea transportation is yet the only form adequate to the needs of the west coast, unless roads could be constructed over which trucks could operate. For many years-this is a suggestion I am going to make, Mr. Speaker-a subsidy has been paid by the federal government to make possible the operation of ships to the west coast for the transfer of passengers and freight to and from these isolated places. It is suggested that consideration be given to the transfer of the amount of this subsidy to another form of communication, particularly to grant a like amount over a limited number of years toward the cost of constructing connecting roads.
One of the vexed questions in my constituency is the problem raised by the presence of large defence establishments, and the operation of very heavy equipment. I know this is a touchy point, but I feel it is necessary to bring it to the attention of the government. I am referring to a particular road in the municipality of Esquimalt which was built and maintained by that municipality but which is used, probably 80 per cent or more, by the heavy equipment of the defence forces. A great deal has been said about military roads, and we each appoint ourselves as chief of the general staff to decide which roads are going to be military roads. Nevertheless, in the particular circumstances which we have here, where a road actually connects two defence establishments and is used almost exclusively by those forces, there seems to be a reasonable case made out for federal assistance in putting that road into first-class shape and keeping it so.
A few words may be in order now, Mr. Speaker, about Canada's position as a trading nation. We have become the third trading

nation in the world. We are a nation of producers, and are dependent upon an active export market. My own province, British Columbia, like the rest of Canada, produces much more than it can consume. It depends for survival upon exports. I am satisfied that the Department of Trade and Commerce is vigorously engaged in seeking outlets for our surplus products, and has made substantial progress in that direction. I confess to a wish, Mr. Speaker, that ways can be found to renew our commercial ties with Great Britain. I am confident that, with the removal of the many restrictions under which those grand people have laboured so long, they will, with their traditional resiliency, rapidly re-establish that leadership which formerly was theirs and which we hope soon to see again. In the meantime, any measures we can take to meet them more than halfway and to hasten the day when our currencies will be mutually acceptable will meet with the approval of the Canadian people.
I am confident that the government will grasp every opportunity to bring this about, and that it will be greatly to our advantage. The fact is that we have surpluses for which we seek markets. May I remind hon. members who have spoken so strongly about surpluses of prairie grains that we in British Columbia have surpluses of lumber and lumber products; of salmon and other fish products; and also of fruit of all kinds from the orchards of the Okanagan. We shall always have such surpluses. With our growing population it ought to be possible to reduce the wide margin which now exists between what we produce and what we consume.
For this reason I wish to associate myself with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall) concerning the formation of a branch or division within the Department of Trade and Commerce charged with the duty of exploring the possibility of stimulating internal and interprovincial trade. I should like to interject here that probably the problem raised by the previous speaker, the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn), who spoke about potatoes coming from California to British Columbia and British Columbia potatoes going from British Columbia to Manitoba, should come within the purview of a department charged with stimulating internal trade.
References have been made to the rising stature of Canada amongst the nations of the world. Not only is this due to the position she occupies as a trading nation, but also to her strong and confident voice in the councils of the nations. I had prepared a few remarks
The Address-Mr. Fairey upon Canada's position as a leading nation in the United Nations and the contribution made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) dealt with that matter fully and eloquently, and I shall omit that part of the remarks I had prepared.
It is gratifying to note that there is general agreement that we should be more generous in helping the less fortunate nations of the world and that it is proposed to increase the amount voted for further assistance under the Colombo plan.
If I may be pardoned a personal reference, may I say very definitely that, as a result of actual experience, I am convinced that the most effective bulwark against communism or any other "ism" is a demonstrated willingness to ease the burden of economic ills which plague so many nations who wish to be our friends.
It was my good fortune, Mr. Speaker, to represent Canada as a member of a three-man educational mission to Burma under the auspices of UNESCO two years ago. During a six-month period I had opportunity to travel throughout that lovely land and also to visit Thailand and India. My conviction is that the training of the nationals of all these countries so that they by themselves may be in a position to develop and expand their own resources by new and improved techniques is the way to that contentment which rejects violent and disturbing forms of government. To assist them to stand on their own feet is, I am sure, the better way.
A word about war veterans allowances. Most of those who have spoken before me in this debate, Mr. Speaker, have referred to the representations made to us by the Canadian Legion, and almost without exception members have declared themselves in favour of the proposals. That is a very easy and popular thing to do. Certainly I shall support any suggestion made by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe), because this department enjoys a reputation for fairness and even generosity to veterans. I agree that some change in raising the ceiling on allowable earnings seems reasonable, but I am concerned about the near approach of these allowances to the amount paid to a veteran in receipt of a disability pension. There is a balance to be maintained.
The national institute for the blind has pointed out what I think is a desirable change in the regulations concerning the allowances paid to the blind. I think the change should be made.
My life, Mr. Speaker, has been spent in the field of education, the greater part of it in technical and vocational education. I suggest

The Address-Mr. Knowles this is of growing importance as Canada develops more and more as an industrial as well as an agricultural nation. The rapid advances in science and technical skills impose a duty upon the government to ensure that we shall always have an adequate, skilled working force, capable of meeting the challenge presented by new inventions and new techniques.
For some years this government has encouraged the expansion of technical training facilities in co-operation with the provinces, in an attempt to keep pace with the demands of industry. It is not a task for the provinces alone. It is my hope that if and when proposals are made for the expansion of this work under the general direction of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), they will provide for the allocation of sufficient funds to make possible notable expansion in the schemes already in effect, and the exploration of new ones.
One final word, Mr. Speaker. It is heartening to hear that proposals are to be made to take care of those suffering total physical handicaps. There will be general agreement to this proposal. There are, however, thousands of men and women suffering from physical handicaps of one kind or another who, with sympathetic care and the right kind of training, can be restored to economic independence, with the concomitant restoration of self-reliance and self-respect. I know that this important matter is under active review. The retraining of persons debarred from their former occupations by physical change is not only right from the humanitarian point of view, but it is economically sound in that it restores to remunerative employment a vast number of persons whose services this country needs.
I am sorry to have taken so long, Mr. Speaker. Thank you.
Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North
Centre): Mr. Speaker, I am sure it must be apparent to this house that we of this group have come back to this parliament not only with a substantial increase in the number of our members, but with some very significant additions to our debating strength. I am sure, too, that the house generally, and the government in particular, knows that we have come to parliament once again with a purpose. That purpose has many aspects, not the least of which is our determination to jolt, jab, prod, poke, pester and attack this government to try to get it to pay some attention to the needs and the wishes of the Canadian people.
I shall make as the main burden of my remarks on this occasion one of the questions
[Mr. Fairey.l

concerning which apparently it is necessary to keep on jolting and jabbing this government; but before I deal with that important question I feel that I should like to say a few words in support of the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). I am sure he had the support of the entire house in his insistence that we in Canada want no part of MeCarthyism, either from the United States or any brand that might be generated in this country itself. We support the position he took with respect to the speech of Mr. Lasky in which he attacked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). I believe the hon. member for Spadina was perfectly justified in asking that no less a person than President Eisenhower repudiate that attack.
It seems to me, however, that there is something more to this whole question than was touched upon this afternoon by the hon. member for Spadina. He may well be correct in his view that the attempt of the people in Washington to get Gouzenko, or an interview with him, is an indirect attack on the Secretary of State for External Affairs or an attempt to blackmail the minister. But I suggest that even more could arise from such an interview. 1 ask hon. members to consider what would happen if Igor Gouzenko were allowed, or allowed himself, to be interviewed by this United States congressional committee, either in the United States or in Canada. What would follow? Does anyone suspect that he is the last Canadian who would be called before such a United States committee? Not on your life. They would call on someone else, and there is no telling who it might be. It might be the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), or the hon. member for Spadina. It might be B. K. Sandwell, Grant Dexter or John Smith off the street. The first of such Canadians who refused to go would immediately be branded as a communist.
I submit that there is in this issue everything the hon. member for Spadina said there was this afternoon, and there is even more. Not only should the Canadian government stand its ground on this issue, but I go so far as to make an appeal to this man Igor Gouzenko, whose whereabouts none of us knows, that he not press, as apparently he has been pressing, for a chance to appear before the United States committee, on television or in any other way.
After all, we have granted to Igor Gouzenko the status of Canadian citizenship, and I submit that he owes a responsibility

to his fellow Canadian citizens to consider what could follow from his actions. According to a dispatch in tonight's Ottawa Citizen apparently there is being run this afternoon in the Toronto Telegram a photostatic copy of a deposition signed by Igor Gouzenko in which he apparently made the statement that he is the one who is asking that the United States committee be permitted to interview him on Canadian soil. This goes even further than the question of the sovereignty of this country. I suggest that if that practice were followed it would place in jeopardy the name and reputation of any Canadian whom any McCarthyite in the United States might choose to criticize or want to call before that committee.
I speak with some particular interest on this question; indeed perhaps I speak from a vantage point enjoyed by few hon. members of this house. I once was a victim of a smear tactic, but as a Canadian I dealt with the matter in the Canadian way. I took it to the courts and a decision was rendered' by the Supreme Court of Ontario, after a jury trial at that, which put a stop to that particular person trying to use his smear tactics against my name and reputation. I submit that all of us in this country prefer that these matters be dealt with in that way. We want no importation of the methods which are causing so much unhappiness, and so much concern amongst thinking people, in the United States at the present time.
I need not go further into this matter because the hon. member for Spadina dealt with it so well and so effectively this afternoon, but I thought he should know, and that the government should know, that the views expressed by him have the support of this house generally.
I indicated earlier that it was my intention in this my first speech in this new parliament to show that we are still the same group we were in the last parliament and' in parliaments before that. We are still here fighting for what we believe is needed and deserved by the Canadian people. We placed at the top of the list of domestic issues when we went to the people in the election of August 10 the need for a nation-wide program of health insurance.
We have placed that need before this house in the form of a subamendment which was moved a few days ago by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I suppose that in the normal course of events, or following the normal pattern of things, as an hon. member referred to it a few moments ago, our subamendment will be beaten when the vote is taken. I
The Address-Mr. Knowles notice a number of Liberal members nodding their heads in agreement with that statement.

That is exactly the point. May I remind hon. members of this house that the first vote of the last parliament took place on September 19, 1949, and that first vote was on the question of abolishing the means test from the old age pension. Every Liberal member who was present in the house stood up and voted against our amendment seeking the abolition of that means test.
That was on September 19, 1949. Before the end of that parliament, due in large part to the jolting and jabbing from this corner of the house, we got rid of the means test on the old age pension, at least at age 70.
It may not be an unhappy omen if our amendment on this occasion is beaten. It may well suggest that before the end' of this parliament the federal government will see the error of its ways and will decide that the time has come to introduce a nation-wide program of health insurance.
This question of health insurance is not a new matter to be brought up on the floor of this house, and my speaking on it certainly is not new. Neither is it a new subject to the Liberal party, or to the Liberal members of this house. As everyone now knows, although many were surprised when we first brought it out five or six years ago, health insurance was first advocated by the Liberals at their convention of 1919. There are members of parliament in this House of Commons today who were not yet born when the Liberal party first promised" health insurance to the Canadian people.
The Liberals did not do very much about it in the earlier years, the twenties and the thirties, although quite a number of speeches were made about it and committees were put to work on it, but in the forties the Liberals did a great deal about health insurance. In fact if I were to detail the whole record it would take more time than is allotted to me.
But I remember the throne speech of 1943. I remember it particularly well because it was the first throne speech I heard as a new member of this house, eleven years ago. On January 28, 1943, the throne speech of that date promised action at that session on the question of a national program of health insurance. Similarly the throne speech the following year, delivered on January 27, 1944, dealt with the question of health insurance.
By this time, of course, there was a little hedging. That throne speech said that when

The Address-Mr. Knowles the provinces were agreeable there would be a program of health insurance submitted to the parliament of Canada. The 1945 throne speech was one of those unusual speeches containing only two paragraphs or so and it did not say so much. Even the long ones do not say very much, for that matter. Health insurance was not inserted in the 1945 throne speech in the earlier part of that year.
However, as everyone knows, it was discussed at length during the election campaign that summer. Liberal members made a great deal of capital out of the fact that in July, 1944, there had been laid on the table of the house in a report by a special committee of the house a draft bill setting out in full detail a national health act.

As my leader points out, it was printed for election purposes despite the fact that the draft bill laid on the table was not really a bill introduced into the house by the government. But as my leader points out, an attempt was made improperly to create the impression that the government had taken action of a legislative character. There it was, and hon. members can find it today in the Journals of this house for July 29, 1944.
In that same year after the election we had the dominion-provincial conference at which the federal government submitted its famous green book proposals which included, among other things, a proposal for national health insurance. Following hard upon the green book proposals of the summer of 1945 came the session of that fall when again in the throne speech, delivered on September 6, 1945, reference was made to the institution of a nation-wide program of health insurance.
It got talked about during all the sessions of that parliament which met from 1945 to 1949, but no action on health insurance then was forthcoming because the government fell back time and again on the argument that the dominion-provincial conference in the summer of 1945 had ended in disagreement. Well, at any rate, as a result of our constant poking at the government over this question we did get something during the life of that parliament. In May of 1948 we got the beginning of the health grants program. Hon. members who were here on that occasion will remember-

Somebody says, "Until the next election". Someone else says, "Another 29 years". Well, as I said a moment ago, I dare to hope that this parliament may repeat what happened at the last one, and that what this house turns down on the first vote of the session becomes law before this parliament is dissolved.
In 1949 there was an election promise that something would be done with respect to health insurance. I do not know whether that promise was circulated widely throughout the country but it certainly was circulated throughout the part of the country from which I come, the city of Winnipeg, where the movement to which I belong is particularly strong.
After that election was over we came back and, lo and behold, reference to health insurance did not appear in the speech from the throne, so we had to start in again fighting for it. Eventually we reached what some of us thought was perhaps the high point up to that time with respect to the question, and I refer to what happened on June 21, 1951. In the previous year we had had a very happy experience in the committee on old age security. Some of us felt that if we could get the same kind of committee, indeed the very same committee as to personnel, to work on the question of health insurance we might get somewhere on this important question. Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was just about to point out that, despite the dismal record of the Liberal party so far as action on health insurance is concerned, that fact did not deter Liberal candidates in last summer's election from campaigning on the issue of health insurance.

The Address-Mr. Knowles
I want to make it quite clear that I have not been able to find a promise of health insurance included in the Liberal party's platform for the election of August 10. I go further, Mr. Speaker, and say that I have not been able to find any Liberal platform. I collected all the Liberal literature that I could collect during the summer months. I collected the advertisements from the newspapers as they appeared, including great big pictures of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), telling what a fine man he was and so on. But at no time did I run across any statement as to the planks in the platform, as to the proposals that the Liberal party was prepared to lay before parliament if it were re-elected. There were many references to what the Liberal party claimed as its record; but alone, among the national parties of this country, it failed to go to the country on the basis of a platform.
However, Mr. Speaker, despite that fact, references were made to health insurance. For example, in one document which was circulated on behalf of the Liberal candidate in my constituency, I found a lengthy paragraph on what the Liberals claim has been done for the health of the Canadian people under the health grants program. Then after a recital of the advantages of that program this sentence appears in italics:	"The national health program is laying the foundation for health insurance." There is no promise that there will be health insurance; there is no plank in the platform to that effect, but there is the suggestion to the electorate that if you vote Liberal, somehow or other, some day, if you live long enough, there will be health insurance.
That same piece of literature to which I have just referred and which I still hold in my hand has on another page this sentence:
The goal of the national health program, Initiated by the St. Laurent government five years ago, is to bring the best of health care within the reach of every Canadian.
I am sure that both the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) would like me to make a slight correction in that statement. Actually the health grants program was initiated by the King government in May, 1948, rather than by the St. Laurent government which took office a few months later. However, Mr. Speaker, there again, without a definite commitment, is the suggestion that if you vote Liberal you will get health insurance. That is what Mr. King said to the country in 1919. That is what has been said by the


Liberals down across these 34 years since it was first put into the platform of the Liberal party.
Despite these references to health insurance that one finds by scraping around in Liberal literature, we come back to this parliament and do we find any reference to it in the speech from the throne? No, there is no reference to health insurance at all. Oh, there is included in the speech from the throne one little promise which the Minister of National Health and Welfare would like us to believe is another step in that direction. I refer to the welcome announcement that there is to be legislation providing for financial assistance to persons who are totally disabled.

I am sure the Minister of National Health and Welfare and indeed the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) would not expect us to go any further at this time than to say that that announcement is welcome. We cannot go any further until we see the details of that legislation. If it is going to involve waiting for legislation by the provinces; if it is going to involve financial negotiations with the provinces before the legislation, provincial and federal, comes into effect; and if perchance there is then to be attached to the legislation a means test, some of our disabled people may yet have a long while to wait before they get the pension which they think, from the throne speech, is coming to them.
However, Mr. Speaker, we welcome that promise; but we suggest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and to the government that this business of inching along toward a proper health program is not good enough for the Canadian people in the light of the needs of our people and in the light of the capacity of this country to establish and support a national health program.
I want to say in passing that I appreciated the friendly remarks-I took them as in that vein, at any rate-of the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais) when he was speaking in French the other day, with reference to a request I had made for financial assistance to families in Manitoba who have been hard hit by the poliomyelitis epidemic that we have had this year. The point the hon. member for Charlevoix made in his speech was, I think, very well taken. I am sorry the Minister of National Health and Welfare did not realize that by this poliomyelitis epidemic there is demonstrated once again the serious shortcoming of any national health

program-such as he calls his health grants program-that does not provide financial assistance to enable people to get health care or to meet a crisis such as many of our people have faced in the province of Manitoba.
At this time we are confronted with hospital costs rising tremendously. Costs of Blue Cross plans throughout this country are rising. The costs of such medical plans as we have are increasing. We have information such as that which was given to us in the government's own sickness survey which shows that the people in the lower income brackets simply are not getting the medical attention they need.
The sickness survey to which I have just referred, just as an example, showed that families with incomes of $5,000 or over are averaging $158.70 a year spent on medical expenses, but where the family has an income of only $1,500 a year or less, the average expenditure is $46.60. No one would deny that the families with lower incomes certainly need just as much medical attention as do those with higher incomes. They probably need more. But because of their inability to pay they are not getting the medical attention which they need and deserve, and which this country is in an economic position to provide.
So, Mr. Speaker, because of the need for health insurance, because of its social desirability, because of the capacity of our country to provide it and because of the commitments that the Liberal party as well as other parties have made with respect to this subject across the years, I submit that this parliament now meeting, this twenty-second parliament of Canada, should not end without the establishment of a national program of health insurance.
As I said in my remarks before supper, one knows the pattern of things around here. That pattern suggests that our subamendment calling for a nation-wide program of health insurance with provision for provincial participation will probably be beaten when the day comes for that vote to be taken. But I say to hon. members on the other side of the house: Vote against this subamendment if you wish, as those of you on the other side of the house voted against our amendment calling for the abolition of the means test from the old age pension in 1949, but sooner or later you will see the day when health insurance will be established in this country.
In our view that step should be taken during the life of this parliament. I tell the government that we of this group will 83276-17
The Address-Mr. Knowles certainly give them no peace until action is taken-until health insurance is established for all Canadians, from coast to coast.
In addition to this extremely important question of health insurance there are a number of other matters, and my time will permit me only to refer to them, which we feel are left-over business from the last parliament and should be dealt with without delay. I have already instanced the first vote in the parliament of 1949 to 1953 which had to do with the removal of the means test from the old age pension. I remind hon. members who were here that the last vote in the twenty-first parliament likewise had to do with old age pensions. We of the C.C.F. moved on that occasion, in May of this year, that the house should express itself as of the opinion that the government should give consideration to increasing the amount of the pensions paid under the Old Age Security Act, the Old Age Assistance Act and the Blind Persons Act to an amount commensurate with today's cost of living.
We suggested in our speeches in support of that amendment that in view of the cost of living as it stood in 1953 as compared with what it was in 1949, when $40 was set as the amount of these pensions, and in view of the increase in our gross national product, the amount of these pensions should be not less than $60. Our amendment was defeated. We heard very little about that during the election campaign from the Liberals. Most of their talk on old age pensions was on what they claimed their government had done. They omitted, of course, any reference to the prodding and jolting it took to get any action. Nevertheless, so far as the people of the country are concerned they are still expecting action on the amount of the old age security pension, old age assistance, and the blind persons pension at the present time.
I say again to Liberal members of the house, don't sit back so satisfied just because you won the election with 48 or 49 per cent of the vote and assume that because the means test is off the old age pension at age 70 there is nothing more to do. Hon. members on the other side of the house know as well as I do that that pension is not going to stay at $40 for the next hundred years or the next twenty years. They know it has to be increased in keeping with the rising value of production in the country. Our plea is that our older people should not be asked to wait indefinitely, to wait until they can no longer keep alive on today's amount, but rather that there should be an increase in the amount of these pensions with the least possible delay.

We feel, too, that the time has come to remove the means test from the old age pension at the age of 65. In that connection, Mr. Speaker, may I say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, before he brings in his promised legislation having to do with pensions for disabled persons, that he should reconsider, if there is any thought of it, this idea of attaching a means test to that pension. Surely in this day and age what we are doing with the means test is to get rid of it. Surely we got over a very important hump when we got rid of the means test from the old age pension at age 70. Let us carry on in the right direction and get rid of it from other statutes of this parliament where it should not be, and let us not introduce it in new, valuable and important legislation such as that providing pensions for disabled or incurable persons.
As I say, time will not permit me to pursue that question at any length, but as hon. members who have been here before are well aware I will have something more to say about old age pension matters as time goes on.
Likewise in just a sentence I want to indicate my continued support for the position taken by the Canadian Legion, particularly with respect to the War Veterans Allowance Act. In my view their claim is one that should be met, namely that the amount of the allowance should be increased to not less than $60 a month single and $120 a month married; and if you cannot get rid of the means test altogether at least the income ceiling should be raised to not less than $1,200 a year single and $2,000 a year married. We will have more to say about these matters of a social security nature as the session goes on.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say this: we feel that when we ask for health insurance, when we ask for adequate old age pensions, when we ask for proper legislation for our veterans, we are not asking that our Canadian people be given something for nothing. We are simply asking that it be recognized that the great wealth of this country is produced by the Canadian people, the workers and farmers who toil and turn our natural resources into real wealth. Because it is our people who produce the wealth of this country we contend that they have a right to get that wealth back in a decent standard of living, in decent and adequate wages where they are industrial workers, in decent and proper prices to our farmers for their products, and in measures of social security such as I have referred to tonight and such as we will continue to fight for during the life of this parliament.


The speech I have made is perhaps a little different from some of the speeches made at the opening of a session. Many speeches these days are including niceties of one kind or another, congratulations to various people and so on, but it seemed to me that what was needed, before the government is allowed to settle down into the complacency of which it is so capable, was to tell the government that some of us in this house are going to carry on this process of jolting and jabbing until we get the progressive kind of legislation to which we believe the Canadian people are entitled.

Mr. Speaker, I too, like a large number of members who have already spoken, would like to extend to you and to your deputy my congratulations on your new appointments. I hope, sir, that your unbiased and objective interpretation of the rules will meet with the cooperation from every member that you deserve.
Having said that, I think I have completed the congratulations which I feel justified in extending at this moment. Before I leave the impression that I look at the whole world with a jaundiced eye I hasten to say that there are a couple of things in the speech from the throne which please me considerably. The first one has to do with something that is being done to aid fishermen, and it is referred to in these words at page 5 of Hansard of November 12, 1953:
The scheme initiated during the last parliament for insuring boats and certain gear has recently been improved and is helping to meet the hazards of the fishing industry.
There is still a lot of room for improvement in that connection. Last year the fishermen in my riding experienced a very severe and unexpected storm which in many cases wiped them out of business completely. I know personally of cases of fishermen who, in the space of 24 hours, were reduced from as many as 800 lobster traps to half a dozen, in the middle of the fishing season.
In the case of these men, insurance on equipment which they may be able to build or purchase in the next year is not good enough. Although this was a limited thing as far as the number of individuals involved, it was just as great a disaster to them as the fires which wiped out some villages in Quebec a couple of years ago, and just as much a tragedy to the individuals concerned as the Winnipeg floods or the tornado in western Ontario. I feel that something more than just a promise of helping these fishermen to insure equipment which they may be able to replace at great expense is needed. I should

like to have seen last year some outright grant made to these people so they would have been in a position to set themselves up in their business again before the end of the fishing season.
I was pleased, too, with the reference made in the speech from the throne to the relief to be afforded to completely disabled persons. The reference is in these words, which appear at page 5 of Hansard for November 12, 1953:
. . . a measure to facilitate the establishment nation-wide of a federal-provincial assistance program for totally disabled persons will be submitted for your consideration.
I am very pleased with that because I have recognized for a long time that people who are physically handicapped by being crippled or disabled in some other way are perhaps equally as entitled to relief as the people who are disabled because of blindness or old age. I am pleased to see that the government contemplates doing something toward relieving their situation.
My main purpose in rising to speak in this debate, Mr. Speaker, is to bring to the attention of this house and the government generally the unsatisfactory conditions which now exist in agriculture in this country, with special reference to the depressed condition of agriculture in Prince Edward Island, the province from which I come. In that connection I should like to quote from the "Current Review of Agricultural Conditions in Canada" for November, 1953. In reviewing the economic conditions of the country generally, this report says on page 5:
Income: The continuing high level of economic activity is reflected in the income components of gross national product. Labour income for the first seven months of this year was 10 per cent higher than in the corresponding period of 1952. This resulted from a small increase in employment accompanied by sizeable increases in wage rates. Average hourly earnings, one of the best available indicators of the basic wage structure, have continued to advance. At July 1, 1953, average hourly earnings in manufacturing industries were 6 per cent over those at the same date in 1952, and increases in other industries ranged between that of mining which was up 4 per cent and building construction where hourly earnings were close to 10 per cent higher. Although the trend in basic working hours has continued downward, more overtime and less short time, particularly in manufacturing, has resulted in slightly longer working hours this year. Along with higher basic rates, the longer work week has contributed to the steady rise in average weekly earnings to their present peak. At July 1 of this year, average weekly salaries and wages stood at $57.58 compared with $53.96 at July 1, 1952.
Further along in this report, Mr. Speaker, the problem of the agricultural industry is mentioned, and I should like to contrast what I have just read with the situation which 83276-174
The Address-Mr. MacLean applies in so far as farm income is concerned. On page 10 of this same review it says:
It is estimated that farm net income from farming operations during 1953 will be about 12 per cent below the 1952 level. This estimate is based on information available up to about the middle of September.
In addition to that, we find that net farm income in 1952 was 11 per cent lower than it was in 1951. There has been a strong downward trend in farm net income over the last two years. It is for that reason that I am deeply disturbed about the economic conditions which now exist in this country so far as agriculture is concerned.
Perhaps it will be said that it does not matter to this house if a few farmers have not as much spending money as they had last year or the year before. Perhaps someone will say, what difference does it make if a few farmers in Prince Edward Island or in the Fraser valley or in New Brunswick are not getting as much for their crops as they have in the past?
My contention is that it is a very important matter for several reasons. In the first place, bad economic conditions in agriculture bear in them the seeds of depression, or at least a severe economic recession. If the purchasing power of the farmer is reduced, the industries which supply the farmer will suffer correspondingly. I believe it is bad business, too, for our western civilization to force farmers out of production by economic pressures, even though they are producing food and clothing at a time when a large percentage of the population of the world is going ill-clad and ill-nourished. From a national point of view, too, it is a bad thing for agriculture to be in an unsound economic condition. I believe it was Booker T. Washington who said that no race could prosper until it learned that there is as much dignity in tilling a field as there is in writing a poem.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that a healthy and prosperous agriculture in this country is of great national importance from the viewpoint of human resources, if for no other reason. It has long been observed that rural populations are, generally speaking, industrious, healthy and well adjusted in their relations with their fellow man. This observation was made as long ago as the first century. I think it was Pliny the Elder who said:
The agricultural population, says Cato, produce the bravest men, the most valiant soldiers, and a class of citizens the least given of all to evil designs.
I noticed some hon. members applauding. I do not say this lightly; I believe it is true.

The Address-Mr. MacLean It is interesting to note that even modern statistics, as recently as last year and applicable to this country, proved that very point. In this country the provinces of Prince Edward Island and Saskatchewan are more dependent upon agriculture than any other province. If you look up the statistics having to do with crime or with almost any other thing, you will find that the provinces of Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island are lowest in those characteristics which are least desirable and highest in the characteristics which are most desirable amongst the general population.
For instance, if you refer to the Canada Year Book for 1952-53, you will notice a table on page 293 headed "Adults convicted of indictable offences, ratio per ten thousand of population". Strangely enough it will be found that Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island have identical figures, 19 per 10,000 of population, and that is by far the lowest for the whole of Canada. Again you will find identical figures for the number of motor vehicle accidents per 10,000 motor vehicles registered in the province. There are many other ways in which this can be proved, if statistics prove anything. But from every point of view it is reasonable to suggest that there is no valid reason why the agricultural people of this country should not share equally and fairly in the material benefits that our economy produces. At the present time that is not so.
As I have already said, in the period of a year preceding last July the net income for agriculture dropped 12 per cent. In the preceding twelve months it dropped 11 per cent, while the average wage earned in industry increased 6 per cent over a period of one year. The unfortunate part of this drop in net income, as far as the people I represent are concerned, is that it is not spread evenly over the whole agricultural economy. By reference again to the "Current Review of Agricultural Conditions in Canada" for November you will find, on page 11, the index of farm prices, the following:
The index for the first seven months would be from 5 to 10 per cent below last year's level. The decline so far this year is largely attributable to significant reductions in the prices of livestock and potatoes and a minor reduction in the price of dairy products.
I may say that the sale of animal products and potatoes is what the farmers of my constituency depend on for their income. At the present time farmers of Prince Edward Island are forced to sell potatoes at a price which is far below the cost of production, and that is a very unfortunate position for them to find themselves in when one realizes that the per capita net value of production


in Prince Edward Island over the last number of years has been consistently lower than that of any other province in Canada.
I grant you there is a principle of economics which says that people are not prone to want to earn their livelihood in places which are undesirable communities in which to live. Therefore conversely if the place is especially desirable as a home, people will accept lower rewards for their efforts in order to have the privilege of living there. For instance, if you want to persuade a native of my province to work and earn his livelihood near the Arctic circle, shall we say, you must offer him pretty high wages. If you were to expect him to work in the tropics you would have to offer pretty high wages; and as far as statistics go, if you were to expect him to work in Toronto you would have to offer him pretty high wages. But I do not think the principle of the desirability of the place in which to live accounts entirely for the great discrepancy between the average income in my province and in other parts of Canada.
As I have already said, this depressed economy now has saddled upon it an absurd load, as far as the selling price of our main cash crop is concerned. I refer of course to potatoes. At the present time the price which is being offered to farmers in Prince Edward Island is 56J cents for a 75-pound bag. That includes the cost of the container. That, as anyone who is acquainted with growing potatoes knows, is an absurd price. I venture to say it costs at least as much to produce a bushel of potatoes as it does to produce a bushel of wheat, and I think more. It would be fair to say that if western farmers were offered 45 cents a bushel for wheat they would refuse to sell, and they would hold their product until the price improved; but the law of supply and demand does not apply strictly to a perishable crop such as potatoes, especially immediately after a crop has been harvested. Potatoes are a very perishable crop and they must be disposed of in a short time. The farmer has no choice; he cannot hold his harvest until the price has improved.
In addition to that, the financial position of many of the farmers in Prince Edward Island is such that, regardless of the price of potatoes, they must sell in order to meet the fixed charges of the cost of growing. The result is that if the price is low it tends to flood the market, because the farmer is forced to sell more potatoes than he normally would if the price were good, in order to meet his bills for fertilizer and other fixed charges, which are very high in the growing of potatoes.

It may be said that I am out to hold up the consumer, to force him to pay exorbitant prices for potatoes, and therefore add to the cost of living. A lot of people who represent city ridings may take that point of view. I would like to point out that the average annual per capita consumption of potatoes in this country is only about 200 pounds. The cost of potatoes, even at a good price to the farmers, is slight as compared with the total number of factors which make up the cost of living. At the present time in Prince Edward Island the farmer is being offered 45 cents a bushel for potatoes. If that price were to be increased from 56} cents a bag to say $1.26} it might be acceptable and would meet the cost of production. It would add only $2 a year to the grocery bill of the average Canadian. I do not think the consumers of this country are so miserly that they want to see the potato-growing industry of this country sabotaged and the potato growers going into bankruptcy in order that they may save 4 cents a week additional on their grocery bills.
I am told that at the present time offerings of potatoes in Prince Edward Island, in New Brunswick and in other growing centres are heavy. They are heavy for the very reason I have already given. Farmers must sell a lot in order to pay their fixed charges. I believe this government should make every effort to educate the Canadian people into being willing to pay fair prices for the basic necessities of life.
Probably owing to high pressure advertising or something else that I cannot account for, there seems to be a tendency among the Canadian people to expect to get the necessities of life at prices so low that they can then afford to pay fancy prices for the luxuries they do not really need. A great many people are willing to pay 30 cents for a quart of beer but they hate to pay 21 cents for a quart of milk. There are large numbers of people in this country who would gladly pay 40 cents for a pack of cigarettes, but they hesitate to pay 5 cents for a pound of potatoes, and potatoes at 5 cents a pound is about the cheapest energy-producing food that is produced in this country.
I am pleased that the potato growers in my province may benefit from action which is now being taken under the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act of 1939. I hope the people who are trying to better their position by means of that act will meet with success. I hope the government will use every possible means at its disposal to see that the producers of essentials in this country get a fair reward for their labour.
The Address-Mr. MacLean
I know the intentions of the government and the Department of Agriculture are good when it comes to compiling crop reports and things of that nature, but I feel that sometimes harm is often done, perhaps inadvertently, to the very people they are trying to help. Perhaps the best example of this is to be found in the September issue of "Current Review of Agricultural Conditions in Canada". At page 24, dealing with fruits and vegetables, reference is made to raspberries and it is estimated that the 1953 raspberry crop of 13,000,000 quarts is 9 per cent greater than the 1952 crop. They then go on to indicate that prices have been generally higher this season than those prevailing last .year. In spite of the increased production, prices went up.
Then in the next paragraph they refer to potatoes. I do not know why the growers of potatoes should be specially victimized, but that seems to be the case. This reads:
The total acreage planted to potatoes is estimated at 320,800 acres. This is 8 per cent and 12 per cent greater than the 1952 and 1951 plantings, respectively. New Brunswick, Ontario and British Columbia report the largest increases, whereas Alberta and Saskatchewan report a decline in acreage. Prices this year have been considerably lower than those prevailing in the same period of 1952. The situation is general throughout Canada and the United States where total production is expected to amount to 376,773,000 bushels or 8 per cent over the 1952 crop.
That may be fair enough down that far, but they then go on to make what I feel is an unjustifiable prediction when they say:
In view of the probable increase in production in both Canada and the United States, it is unlikely that prices will reach the levels of the 1952-53 season.
That is an open invitation to the trade. It is telling them that the potato producers of North America are stuck with more potatoes than they can get rid of and there is an opportunity to buy potatoes from the farmers at the lowest possible prices. As I said before, when the trade attempts to do that the law of supply and demand breaks down because potatoes are a perishable product and the farmers must dispose of them immediately. They must glut the market in order to acquire enough cash to satisfy their fixed charges.
That statement is most unfortunate when one realizes that in the next issue of the same review for November they say in effect, "we are sorry, we estimated a little too high; the crop is not as big as that after all. It is only 6 per cent greater than it was last year." Although that statement may have been unintentional it had a depressing effect upon the market for potatoes in this country.

The Address-Mr. MacLean
The general result of this situation is that economic conditions in my province are very bad. The city of Charlottetown is dependent for its prosperity upon the prosperity of the farmers and at the present time it is in the depths of a local depression. There is a chronic unemployment situation there. On October 22 of this year there were 735 people in Charlottetown for whom jobs could not be provided. In addition, 267 people in Queens and Kings counties had been placed in jobs outside the province during the first six months of this year. Likely there would be a similar number placed in the last six months. That would bring the actual unemployment figure for those two counties up to something like 1,400. In addition there would be at least 1,000 more people who have gone off under their own steam to Toronto, Edmonton, Seven Islands or some place like that to seek employment. In actual fact you have a grave unemployment situation in Prince Edward Island.
Immediately after the war we heard a great deal about the shelf of reserve projects and public works which were to be used immediately soft spots occurred in the economy of our country and the unemployment figures began to rise. Time and time again the people of Charlottetown have been promised a new, up-to-date, modern federal office building. I am encouraged by the recent announcement of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) to the effect that an item will be provided in the estimates this year to begin the construction of a new federal building in Charlottetown. Although the reward which the people of rny riding receive for their labours is lower on a per capita basis than that of any province in Canada, it does not mean that their production is lower. The people of my province are hard-working, efficient people. They are farmers for the most part, although there are some fishermen and men of other walks of life. The rewards received for their efforts have been discouraging.
The farmers of my province have not only attempted to earn a decent living for themselves by hard work, but have tried to pass on their farms to their descendants in at


least the same condition they were in when they received them from their ancestors. That is a worth-while ambition, and it is a good omen for the conservation of our natural resources.

Mr. Speaker, I would first like to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) and the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Villeneuve) for the capable and able manner in which they moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I represent the people of the riding of Waterloo South, which is composed of the township of North Dumfries, the township of Wilmot, and part of the township of Waterloo; the city of Galt, the towns of Preston and Hespeler, and a number of other small villages and rural communities. Nearly all of the riding which I represent lies in the watershed of the Grand river and its tributaries. If you were to pass through this riding you would see rolling hills and valleys with the Grand river and its tributaries making picturesque scenes of outstanding beauty.
The well cultivated and rolling farmlands, with their well kept homes and barns, indicate at once to the visitor the fertility of the soil and the industry of the farming population. There are also in my riding urban centres that are very progressive and heavily industrialized. As a matter of fact the county of Waterloo, which is divided into the north and south ridings, and the surrounding areas including the city of Guelph and the city of Brantford, constitute one of the most heavily industrialized parts of Ontario.
The expansion of existing industries, combined with the establishment of new industries in this area during this period of economic growth that Canada has been experiencing, has created many new and trying problems for the municipalities. One is the shortage of housing accommodation, and I am glad to see that the government, recognizing that a shortage of homes still
The Address-Mr. A. W. A. White exists in Canada, has indicated in the speech from the throne provisions to alleviate this condition.
We in the Grand river watershed pride ourselves upon being the first group of municipalities to unite for conservation work.
As a result, the Grand river conservation commission was formed and the Shand and Luther dams were built by this commission to ameliorate the disastrous flooding conditions which existed in the watershed during the spring run-off, and to increase the summer flow to flush out the river channel during times of low water. Last year this government, in co-operation with the provincial government, approved the building of a $5 million dam at Glen Allan, which is the final dam to be built in this scheme. When it is completed the flood waters of the Grand river and its tributaries, the experts tell us, will be harnessed. I would at this time, on behalf of the people in the Grand river watershed, like to thank the government of Canada for their financial assistance in these projects.
The people of the riding of South Waterloo have also shown the people of Canada how to unite for their common good in another field. On August 11 of this year a new 177-bed hospital was officially opened in the city of Galt, known as the South Waterloo Memorial hospital. This is a district hospital.
Its capital cost and maintenance are being shared on a per capita basis by the residents of the township of North Dumfries, the town of Preston, the town of Hespeler and the city of Galt; so that the cost of hospitalization in this part of South Waterloo will be equally distributed between all the people for whose benefit the hospital with its modern facilities was erected.
I would like to tell you that this hospital is completely furnished and equipped with all the latest and most up-to-date technical equipment that is on the market, and the entire cost of these furnishings and equipment was raised by public subscription in the participating municipalities. I would at this time, on behalf of the people in my riding, like to thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and this government, as well as the provincial government, for their grants which helped to make this long-needed hospital accommodation possible.
There is a matter that is causing grave concern to all people in the Grand river watershed, and that is the fact that the Grand river has become the No. 1 pollution problem in the province of Ontario. This is
due to the rapid growth of urban centres
264	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. A. W. A. White along its banks and the inadequacy of sewage treatment plants, or the lack of them altogether in some cases, to cope with and treat properly the increased amount of sewage and industrial waste. This government will be asked, if they have not been asked already, by the anti-pollution committee of the Grand river conservation authority to join with the municipalities and the provincial government and to assist financially in cleaning up this condition. I know that my friend and colleague the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) will agree with this statement, because the people of the city of Brantford have to get their drinking water out of the Grand river and are put to additional expense because of present conditions.
As the representative of the people of Waterloo South in the parliament of Canada, I feel it is my duty to bring to the attention of the government matters that are vitally important to my constituents as well as to many citizens throughout the entire Dominion of Canada. Therefore I bring to your attention another serious problem with which many workers and manufacturers are confronted not only in my riding but throughout the length and breadth of this great country.
I speak, of course, of the present condition of the textile industry in Canada.
This industry, at its peak in April, 1951, employed 104,000 men and women. By July, 1952 the number of persons employed had dropped to 82,328. In April, 1953, employment went up to a new level of 95,000 persons. Since that time this figure has gradually dropped until today the number of men and women employed in this basic industry has been reduced to 85,000 persons. This drop of 10,000 persons employed in this industry in the last seven months does not, however, tell the whole story because a large number of these people are on short time, as low as two and three days a week.
To get back to my own riding of Waterloo South, I have gathered the following information. The Staufler-Dobbie mill normally employing 450 people is now employing 300 workers at the height of its rush season; and from April to September of this year this mill was operating on short time of three to four days a week. The Riverside silk mill employing over 200 workers is now operating at only two-thirds of this capacity. The Turnbull mill employing 200 workers is now operating at 80 per cent of this capacity on short time of two to three days a week. The Newlands mill normally employing 500 workers is now employing only 350 persons on three and a half to four days a week. The 

Galt Knitting Company is operating on short time with only one-third of its normal number of employees.
In the neighbouring town of Hespeler, which has a population of approximately 3,900, the large Dominion woollen mill normally employs 1,100 persons and the Artex woollen mill normally employs 315 persons. These two mills between them normally provide employment for 1,415 people out of a total population of 3,900. Today the Dominion woollen mill is employing 700 persons and even this number is experiencing considerable short time. The Artex woollen mill is now operating and employing only 215 persons, a drop of 30 per cent. Of 54 looms the company is operating only 36 at the present time. These are some facts and figures showing the position of the textile industry in my riding, and I know the same situation exists in the textile industry throughout the entire Dominion of Canada.
In the year 1950 the Canadian textile mills manufactured 68 per cent of all the requirements of the Canadian people. In the early part of this year this figure had dropped to 52 per cent, and in the last six months the imports have exceeded all previous records and for the first time Canadian mills are now producing less than one-half the total requirements.
I know this government has for some time been aware of the serious condition of the textile industry in Canada, and has been considering ways and means of remedying and correcting these disturbing conditions. I know the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) has had his department working overtime to prevent goods, sold at depressed prices in the United States and other countries, from finding their way into the Canadian market, and that the anti-dumping laws are being applied wherever possible. But in spite of this fact the situation in the textile industry in Canada is getting progressively worse.
I should like to point out that the textile industry alone in the city of Galt and the town of Hespeler carries a payroll of $5 million a year; and I know the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) especially would like to see full employment prevail-as would all of us in this house-in this and all other industries.
I was highly pleased to see that the speech from the throne indicated that this government is considering amendments to the Customs Act which, I presume, will attempt to alleviate the serious condition which prevails in the textile industry. One suggestion

is -that this amendment should establish that the value for duty on new or unused goods shall not be less than the actual cost of production of these goods in the country of origin plus a reasonable advance for selling cost and profit. There are other methods which could be adopted, too, and I am satisfied that the government will take the necessary action under the circumstances. I should like to suggest that all imported fabrics of any kind should be marked with a label indicating in French or in English the country of origin so that our Canadian consumers can, if they so desire, make sure they are purchasing goods produced in our own country by Canadian workers.
Another disturbing influence in this already serious situation was the recent announcement that Japan has been invited to participate fully in the meetings and in the work of the contracting countries to the general agreement on tariffs and trade. This announcement has been interpreted as granting Japan full GATT membership and extending to that country most-favoured-nation treatment.
This interpretation, I understand, is not correct. I understand that Japan has only been invited to participate on a temporary and provisional basis until the middle of 1955, and that those countries which wish to do so may join in an agreement with Japan to exchange most-favoured-nation treatment and to have GATT govern their commercial relations, but that this government has not undertaken to exchange most-favoured-nation treatment with Japan, nor have they entered into any agreement as yet. I am sure the (government, in negotiating an agreement with Japan, will be mindful of the difference in the standards of living prevailing in the two countries and the difference in wages paid, which could result in disastrously unfair competition in the marketing of Japanese goods in this country. I am also sure the government, mindful of past experience in this regard, will include every safeguard to protect Canadian industry and Canadian workers.
Another matter I should like to mention for a moment is the war veterans allowance, which I feel either should be increased or the veteran should be permitted to supplement his allowance with casual earnings to a greater extent than he is today. I also believe that the total amount of assets a blind person is able to have under the present means test should be increased. But what is more important, in my opinion, is that persons receiving the blind pension should be allowed
The Address-Mr. Herridge to supplement this pension with casual earnings to a greater extent than they are permitted to do under present legislation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, with all modesty I should like to point out to the house that I am the first Liberal to be elected to the federal parliament from Waterloo South since 1896, and I attribute my own election to a great extent to the fine leadership given to the Liberal party and the government of Canada by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) over the past number of years.
