Mr. Deputy Speaker, before proceeding with the few vitally important things I wish to say this evening, I must take this opportunity through you to congratulate Mr. Speaker and yourself. I have seen occasions when a motion to elect a Speaker was somewhat of a formal procedure. There is no question about it that in the case of Mr. Speaker and yourself it was a heartfelt expression of appreciation of your abilities and your service in the past, and best wishes to you both for a successful period in office. I think I entered this parliament the same year as both you gentlemen did and although I am a lesser light of that class I am coming along very well now. I am getting an increasing number of letters addressed to me as "right honourable". Of course I write back to my constituents and thank them for the courtesy, telling them they are somewhat premature but possibly the title will be fit and proper after the next election, when this party is in power.
Now, Mr. Speaker, before proceeding I must congratulate the hon. member for Spa-dina (Mr. Croll) on the most excellent speech he made this afternoon. I think when he spoke he said what all the members of the house are thinking, and what all decent Canadians will support regardless of party.
Coming from a farming community and being a peasant farmer myself, I must say that I heartily support the remarks made the other day by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) with respect to the place of the farming community in the national life of this country and the characteristics of the rural people. I was much heartened again this evening to hear a very similar eulogy of the agricultural population of this country from the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean).
I rise to support the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I endorse the remarks he made prior to moving that amendment, and support
266	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Herridge it. You know, Mr. Speaker, that we members in this group are not given to unnecessary repetition, so I am going to simply conclude, as far as that is concerned, by saying that I most heartily support the policies and the program enunciated by the member for Rosetown-Biggar when he presented the over-all picture.
At the last election this movement presented a ten-point program to the Canadian people. I am not going to deal with all ten points this evening, but I want particularly to draw attention to two or three of them in the course of my remarks.
The first point was that we said if we were elected we would urge this government to give Canadian leadership for peace in eliminating the hunger and poverty on which communism thrives, to build collective security, and support the United Nations and its principles. We intend to do exactly that.
Before I proceed I think it is only fair, although he is not present in his seat tonight, to congratulate the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), and I am duty bound also to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) for the splendid way they represented Canada at the United Nations.
We all must realize that world peace is essential for Canada's future happiness and prosperity, and I am sure all of us are very much heartened by the lessening of tensions in the world, by the Korean armistice, and by the rather heartening things that have been said by very important people in the world on this subject. I am also heartened to see that I have the rapt attention of the member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). When we have the opportunity to discuss external affairs there is no question but that this group will clearly indicate its support for Canadian leadership for peace.
Before leaving the question of international affairs, which I will only mention very briefly, I do want to quote a few words from the remarks of Sir Winston Churchill when he was speaking to the Conservative party conference at Margate, England', on October 10. I quote them because I heartily agree with them and I think, whatever our views in this house are, the majority of members will support them. I think they are well worth while placing on the record and I intend to do so. Sir Winston Churchill on that occasion said:
My prime thought is to simplify. We have lived through half a century of the most terrible events which have ever ravaged the human race. The vast majority of all the peoples, wherever they may dwell, desire above all things to earn their daily bread in peace. To establish conditions under
[Mr. Herridge. 1

which they can do this and to provide deterrents against aggression are the duties confided by the heart's desire of mankind to the United Nations.
I am sure every one of us can say amen to that.
Our first duty is to aid this world instrument loyally and faithfully in its task. But the world also needs patience. It needs a period of calm rather than vehement attempts to produce clear-cut solutions. There have been many periods where prompt and violent action might have averted calamities. This is not one of them. Even if we entered on a phase only of easement for five or ten years, that might lead to something still better when it ended . . .
Five months ago on May 11, I made a speech in the House of Commons. I have not spoken since. This is the first time in my political life that I have kept quiet for so long. I asked for very little. I held out no glittering or exciting hopes about Russia. I thought that friendly, informal, personal talks between the leading countries mainly involved might do good and could not easily do much harm, and that one good thing might lead to another. This humble modest plan, announced as the policy of Her Majesty's government, raised a considerable stir all over the place, and though we have not yet been able to persuade our trusted allies to adopt it in the form I suggested, no one can say it is dead.
I still think that the leading men of the various nations ought to be able to meet together without trying to cut attitudes before excitable publics or using regiments of experts to marshal all the difficulties and objections. And let us try to see whether there is not something better for us all than tearing and blasting each other to pieces, which we can certainly do.
Her Majesty's government, as Mr. Eden and Lord Salisbury told you on Thursday, still believe that we should persevere in seeking such a meeting between the heads of governments.
We in this group most wholeheartedly support that perseverance.
If I stay on for the time being bearing the burden at my age. it is not because of love for power of office. I have had an ample feast of both. If I stay, it is because I have the feeling that I may, through things that have happened, have an influence on what I care about above all else-the building of a sure and lasting peace.
Let us then go forward together with courage and composure, with resolution and good faith to the end which all desire.
I am sure all of us can agree with Sir Winston Churchill's remarks in that connection on the question of world peace.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the second point in our program was to urge the government to establish an immediate nation-wide health insurance program. I am not going to speak at any length on that subject. I endorse wholeheartedly the very lucid explanation of the situation made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) this afternoon. In this case it would be quite fitting and proper for me to say simply amen to the things he said.
Before leaving that subject I do want to say that not only the members of this group but I know a good many members on the

government side of the house in their hearts support the proposal for a national health insurance plan. There is a large body of responsible opinion urging such a program in this country. Some of these people have made a close study of the question; some have dedicated their whole lives to the question of welfare. I should like to quote briefly from the magazine Welfare, the issue for November 1 of this year. This is what the editorial has to say:
Health Care a Necessity
Every now and then, and far too frequently, someone is quoted in the daily press as saying that Canada just does not have enough hospitals or enough doctors to establish any national plan for health services: all further discussion of health insurance, in the face of this fact, is supposed to be futile. What the person is really saying is that health services are now scarce: there is not enough of this commodity to go around, and hence we should let supply and demand determine who gets what-or any.
When essential commodities are in short supply- such as foods in time of war-we decide that their distribution should be controlled by rationing or that the government, with the full approval of the people, should get busy to ensure that the requisite amount is available. Are we to consider health services a luxury, available only in limited quantities to those who can afford to pay for them? Or can we not act on the modern idea that health care is a necessity? The health of the nation is decidedly the nation's business.
Our federal government, in the health grants, has taken some action to increase the supply of health facilities and personnel and the provinces have taken almost full advantage of the offer. This, however, is not enough. The Canadian Welfare Council's committee on health services has reached agreement on the following points:
"A healthy population is one of the objectives of any country ... In order that a country may have a healthy population, it should accept as a goal that health services essential to his needs should be provided and be accessible to each person, and that the country should establish a program designed to meet this goal . . . Each person's ability to maintain or improve his own health is controlled by the availability of the medical facilities and personnel which he needs, and by his financial ability to make use of them . . ."
Now, that is an editorial published by people who made a particular study of the question of the health needs of the people of Canada, and we in this group wholeheartedly support those views.
Another point in our program, No. 3, is a social security program to include sickness benefits, old age pensions and family allowances at adequate rates. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre dealt at some length with this question this afternoon. As I said before, I am not going to repeat his argument. We endorse wholeheartedly what he had to say. When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre speaks, whether it is upon national health insurance, old age pensions or family allowances, I notice it provokes the attendance of the Minister of 83276-184
The Address-Mr. Herridge National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), because it is recognized that the hon. member speaks only after making a full study of the situation and with great sympathy for those who suffer from the lack of these services.
I am going to take a little time to deal particularly with the question of the war veterans of this country, those who are in need of some amendments to the legislation to improve their lot. We in this group are particularly interested in the welfare of the veteran. To demonstrate that point I shall tell a little story. On one occasion a senior officer of the battalion with which I served overseas, who was formerly a colonel in the Indian army, took the chair at one of my meetings. Before he started the meeting he got up to explain his presence to the people by saying:	"Now, ladies and gentlemen, I want (to make my position quite clear. I am not a member of the C.C.F., in fact like a good many people in Canada I am rather foggy about the things for which the group stands. I do know, however, that the C.C.F. take a particular interest in the two problems in which I am particularly interested, the welfare of the veterans and the fruit growers. It is on that account that I occupy the chair for my good friend this evening."
I believe that illustrates our attitude on this question. When I listen to arguments in connection with war veterans allowances and improvements in the pension legislation, I willingly admit, first of all, that we have some excellent veterans legislation to this country. We have every reason to be proud of the progress we have made in that connection. I think we have led the world to that regard, so far as any democratic country is concerned, with our pension act, our rehabilitation act and our War Veterans Allowance Act, with which we have tried to do something for the veterans of the first and second world wars.
I readily agree that that legislation is something to be proud of, in general. I admit the officials who administer that legislation do so very fairly. I have had a great deal to do with the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and I find them anxious to do all they possibly can for the veteran within the terms of the act or the regulations attached thereto. We in this group think, however, as do many other hon. members, that we in Canada can do better than we have done to date. We feel that we can do some of the things the Canadian Legion is asking this house to do.
Whenever I speak on this subject I see in my mind some of the men who served with me in the first world war. I was rather a young man then, but I notice these men are

The Address-Mr. Herridge getting a bit more frail every day. I think of those men who volunteered to defend this country, without any question, when the call came. I come from a community, Mr. Speaker, in which 124 men out of a total population of 1,422 people joined the colours within a few months. A good many of those men returned. They are ageing, and I never speak on this subject without seeing in my mind some of those chaps doing the best they can to get along on the war veterans allowance, their pension or possibly trying to make their living in other ways. I think of the addresses to which I listened, as I expect other hon. members did, when they were in France.
I remember listening to the late Sir Sam Hughes, and I expect the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) remembers as well, when he addressed our division in France, and the glorious future he promised all veterans who returned to this country. The same is true of the late Sir Robert Borden, and in fact of all those gentlemen who went over there at that time. They promised us everything but the moon. I think I am correct in saying that I remember those promises. I will admit that a great deal has been done, and we in this group are simply asking today that just a little bit more be done to make this legislation as satisfactory as it should be.
I am going to deal somewhat at length with the brief of the Canadian Legion, because to us it is a very important question. I hold in my hand the brief presented to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) and the cabinet by the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League on November 10, 1953. I am not going to read the whole brief, but I do wish to bring to the attention of the house certain things mentioned in it. I recognize that from sea to sea I have attention. I have the attention of the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) from the Atlantic coast, and of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) from the Pacific coast. My ambition is completely satisfied.
I now deal with the brief. I must say we all recognize that the Canadian Legion is a responsible body. It does not ask for the impossible. The Canadian Legion considers its proposals thoroughly. These proposals spring from the rank and file, from the branches throughout the country, the zone councils, the provincial commands and from the dominion conventions. These ideas are condensed in the form of a brief and presented annually to the cabinet of this country.
I suppose it is correct to say that amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act


are of first concern to the veterans' organizations of this country and to the veterans generally. I find in their representations to the cabinet in this connection the Legion representatives recommended this:
That the basic rate of war veterans allowance be increased to $60 per month for a single veteran, and $120 per month for those who are married.
In their comment they had this to say:
The arguments in support of this recommendation have been so frequently stated that they scarcely require to be repeated at this time.
How true. I continue:
Briefly they are:
1. The war veteran has always been recognized by the Canadian people and by successive Canadian governments as meriting very special consideration, and there is, therefore, no likelihood of serious criticism if W.V.A. rates are higher than those payable under old age pension or similar social legislation.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that under existing rates a veteran who must depend on war veterans allowances is suffering actual privation. I know myself of cases of many veterans in receipt of very small disability pensions who are incapable of accepting employment, but are forced to live at less than subsistence levels because of low war veterans allowance rates.
When it comes to the question of financing these proposals, Mr. Speaker, we in this group do not believe in suggesting amendments to legislation and at the same time also suggesting the lowering of taxes. We know that everything has to be paid for. I am speaking personally on this point. During the last session we took the stamp tax off cheques. In that way the government saved about $10 million for the Canadian people, because it was no longer necessary to put stamps on cheques, receipts and certain documents of that sort. To put a stamp on a cheque is not a hardship to the average Canadian, because the average Canadian does not issue many cheques. It might have had an effect on some people but it was not any great hardship to any large number of people. Therefore I think we could have very well retained the stamp cheque tax and the necessity to purchase stamps for cheques, receipts and other documents, and use the $10 million saved in that way to give the war veterans improvements in the war veterans allowance that the Canadian Legion asked for.
The second recommendation of the Legion is:
That the ceilings on total permissible income under W.V.A. be increased to $1,200 per year in the case of a single recipient and $2,000 per year in the case of those married.

The comment is as follows:
Again, supporting arguments have been stated at frequent intervals and such statements would appear to be as valid today as when originally put forward.
These statements have been made repeatedly in this house. I do offer the suggestion to the government that if at this stage they cannot see fit to increase the war veterans allowance-we are urging they do- as a first step in the early days of this session amendments to the legislation be brought down so that the ceilings on total permissible income can be increased according to the recommendation of the Canadian Legion. That would meet the position of quite a number of these men in the country at this time.
The third recommendation was as follows:
That where an allowance is granted on behalf of an incapacitated child over the age of 21, the allowance be continued on the death of the parent.
The reason for that was this:
Special allowances are provided under section 12
(2)	of the act for children prevented by physical or mental incapacity from earning a living. The section makes no provision for the child, however, in the event of death of the surviving parent.
That is a very reasonable suggestion and would mean small additional expense to the exchequer of this country.
The fourth recommendation reads:
That allowances on behalf of minor children of W.V.A. recipients be paid on the same basis as such allowances are now paid to the children of disability pensioners.
The reason given for that is:
While there are veterans over 60 in receipt of the allowance who would certainly benefit by this change, it is particularly essential in the case of the veteran under 60 who is in receipt of W.V.A. because he is incapacitated. In some cases the veteran in this category is trying to support a wife and several small children on $90 per month.
I can illustrate the need for the amendment suggested by the Canadian Legion by a case in my own constituency. There was a veteran who was completely incapacitated. He had two little girls. They were very bright. He wants them to go to high school and university. His wife went to work parttime as a stenographer to provide funds to meet the cost of these children's university education. She carried on for a couple of years, and then they discovered that there was an overpayment of some $1,800. According to the law the veteran is required to make repayment.
I must say the board was very fair. They made the repayment as small as possible, according to the legislation and the regulations; but it is to cover such situations that the Legion asks for this amendment. As an
The Address-Mr. Herridge hon. member in front of me suggests, it stopped the wife working. That means that it is very difficult indeed for these two bright young Canadian girls to continue with their university education. Surely a man who has served his country to such an extent that he is at present incapacitated and unable to work is not going to be denied the opportunity of having his children obtain the education their ability warrants.
Recommendation No. 5 reads:
That any necessary amendments should be made to sections 3 and 30 (11) of the act so that a woman who resided with a veteran during his lifetime may be granted an allowance in the event of her surviving him, if the circumstances are such that if the veteran had, immediately prior to his death applied for an allowance as a married man, he would for that purpose have been deemed to have been married to such woman and would have been granted such allowance.
I have run into one or two cases of that kind myself. The Legion recommendation is based on very sound ground indeed.
Then recommendation 6:
That perquisites be not considered as income under the act.
The comment of the Legion is:
We suggest that W.V.A. recipient who cuts his' own wood and keeps his own cow and chickens, should not have the value of the resulting produce deducted from his W.V.A. Why discourage the recipient from contributing to the general production of goods and services?
I am sure that is a reasonable proposition. I have numbers of these men in my own constituency who live in small houses, in some cases log cabins. They have a pig or two, and possibly a cow. They cut their own wood because there is plenty of standing timber in that country, and according to the act it is all considered as income. I think these men should be encouraged to do that sort of thing. We talk about free enterprise, individual initiative and so on. I have in my constituency one old chap 85 years of age who cuts all his own wood, keeps a pig or two and a cow, and cultivates a good garden. By having made some income because he is willing to work and add to the production of this country by providing for his own maintenance he is denied any allowance. I think the Legion is on very sound ground when it suggests that amendment to the legislation.
Recommendations 7 and 8 read:
7. Recommendation.
That the somewhat arbitrary regulation of W.V.A. whereby one-half of the gross income from a small holding is considered net income, be amended to permit the recipient, if he so desires, to charge all legitimate expenses against gross income as provided for by the Income Tax Act.
Comment. The W.V.A. regulation as it stands may provide a useful, rough and ready yardstick in many cases, but can and does prove unjust where labour must be hired.
270	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Herridge
8. Recommendation.
That Canadian veterans resident outside of Canada and otherwise qualified, be granted war veterans allowance.
Comment. Many veterans of the Canadian forces have found it necessary (for health reasons- possibly due to pensionable disabilities) to reside outside of Canada. We feel that these veterans should not be denied the right to war veterans allowance. The numbers are small and the cost would not be great if this recommendation were acted upon.
I have the case of a man in my constituency who worked in Trail for years, but he suffers from a lung disability and must go south for a month or two every year. I heartily support that recommendation of the Canadian Legion.
Recommendation 9 follows:
That the provisions of section 5 of the W.V.A. act be made retroactive to January 1, 1952.
Comment. Section 5 of the War Veterans Allowance Act, as amended in 1952, makes provision for the payment of W.V.A. at married rates to the survivor for 12 months following death of either the veteran or his wife, where W.V.A. was being paid at such rate prior to death. This section, however, has been interpreted to mean that the benefit cannot be extended to the surviving party where death occurred between January 1, 1952, and July 4, 1952.
Then I go on to recommendation 11 which reads:
That veterans of world war I who saw service in England only be granted W.V.A.
That has been asked for repeatedly by the Canadian Legion and the request has been repeatedly rejected. During the second world war Great Britain was considered a theatre of war, but in world war I according to our regulations it was not a theatre of war. We think it is high time that we extended war veterans allowances to those veterans, whose numbers are rapidly decreasing, who served during the first world war but who were sent only to England. In many cases they were acting under instructions and had to stay in England.
Those are all the comments I wish to make with reference to war veterans allowances.
I am not going to deal with the Pension Act because my time will not permit. In the meantime I want to say a few words on housing. The C.C.F. has urged a national housing program to provide 100,000 new homes a year. We talk about housing from year to year, but the problem continues to grow and increase. I could read comments which have appeared in the local press of my constituency, in the Vancouver press and in the British Columbia press indicating the great need for housing.
I attended a Legion convention, of the Kootenay branch, in Nelson just before coming down to the house, and the major


topic at that convention was the need for housing for veterans in Kootenay West. We in this group claim that the present housing legislation will not meet the needs of the people of this country. We consider that the need for housing is a national emergency. We believe that a strong nation can be built only on a satisfactory home life, and good housing is necessary for a satisfactory home life. That is why we believe that national credit through the Bank of Canada should be used to permit the making of loans at 2 per cent with a 10 per cent down payment and the balance repayable over a period of 30 years.
We believe that more should be done to support those in this country who are interested in co-operative industry. I was doing some reading in this connection and I came across a most interesting bit of Canadian history which I should like to refer to at this point. According to the Journals of the House, in February, 1907, a special committee commenced sitting to consider Bill No. 2, respecting industrial and co-operative societies. On March 26, His Excellency the Governor General appeared before the committee to give his views on the question and made some suggestions with respect to the redrafting of the bill. At page 100 of the Journals of the house 1906-07, appendix No. 3, I find a most interesting comment by His Excellency who had previously criticized the legislation that was before the committee. This rather took my eye because I am always interested in odd things. His Excellency said:
I would have you reflect on the security which the development of co-operative methods offer against the tyranny of trusts and combines.
If His Excellency were alive today he would be joining this group:
There is no guarantee that the power of a trust, or a combine, will not be used against the general well-being of both producers and consumers. The co-operative movement provides a safeguard against this danger of a value proportionate to its strength.
He later went on to give some interesting information to the committee concerning cooperative housing, and his concluding remarks appear on page 102 as follows:
I have put this information before the committee owing to a remark of Mr. Verville leading me to suppose that the problem of how to house the workmen of the rising towns of Canada is one which is very naturally engaging his attention.
The point I wish to make is that a housing situation existed in 1907 which caused His Excellency the Governor General to come before a special committee of this house to make suggestions regarding co-operative housing. It was a problem in 1907 and it is a problem today. Apparently we have not

The Address-Mr. Herridge
made much progress in this connection. The problem existed in 1907 and we are still discussing a housing program for Canada.
I suggest that the government give every consideration to promoting and assisting cooperative housing. When I finish with this book I suggest to hon. members that they get it and read what His Excellency had to say about co-operative housing as practised at that time in Great Britain and other countries.
I should like to deal briefly with the suggestions of the Legion in connection with housing, and they have made some very interesting ones. There is no doubt that this is important so far as the veterans of this country are concerned. When they presented their case to the cabinet the representatives of the Legion made some interesting proposals which I do not have the time to deal with at length.
I want to see if I am a good guesser. I think the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is sincerely interested in this problem. I predict that he will be so interested in these proposals that before this session is over the government will introduce legislation along the lines suggested by the Canadian Legion in their brief. I cannot understand why any government would not.
There are over 300 veterans in my constituency who are denied access to the small holdings provisions because they cannot obtain the necessary land. They must obtain three acres; and around the cities of Trail and Nelson it is impossible to get three acres in most cases. But they could get half an acre, which is quite sufficient. Because they are unable to comply with the regulations they are denied the opportunity to benefit from the Veterans Land Act.
They have asked me to urge that the acreage be reduced from three acres to one-half acre as it was before. I see the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) supports me in that, and I would expect the support of the other members for British Columbia as well as the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart). We generally agree on things that are obvious.
Anyway, Mr. Speaker, I would like the members of this house to read the proposals of the Canadian Legion in connection with housing, made on November 10. They are most interesting. They say this at page 4 of the brief;
The V.L.A. administration has cut a pattern for the "build your own home" program and its
experience with over 6,000 houses has enabled them to work the "bugs" out of it. It has a nationwide organization which, while very small, has the experience and training necessary to assure that a more generally applicable scheme could be made to work satisfactorily.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that in my constituency the Veterans Land Act administration conducted schools where veterans were taught to assemble material, dig basements and read plans. They were given general instruction with regard to building a home. The schools were most successful and were appreciated by the veterans in my constituency. A number of those veterans have built under the scheme. The veteran is his own contractor and receives money from the department. After receiving instruction from the school he is processed and obtams a loan provided he can get the necessary three acres of land upon which to erect a home.
I cannot deal at any further length with the schools, Mr. Speaker, but I do support the proposals made by the Canadian Legion. They recommend that the facilities of the Veterans Land Act administration be made available to carry out a build your own home program for city-sized lots on the following terms;
(1)	A veteran to be eligible must have service which would qualify him for settlement under V.L.A.
(2)	The veteran must have title to a suitable lot supplied with water, or sufficient funds to purchase such a lot; the lot to be turned over to the director as security for original advances and should the appraised value of the lot be less than $800, the veteran to deposit the difference with the director.
(3)	A veteran, to qualify, must have a good employment record over a period of at least 4 years, must have taken a course in house construction using the V.L.A. syllabus and standards, and be approved as qualified to take a contract to build his home.
(4)	The veteran must be able to furnish a bond of indemnification to the director, payable in case of loss or misuse of material supplied and paid for by the director on delivery and before it is incorporated in the house.
(5)	The veteran's plan must be approved as being practical and giving good value, and the veteran must agree to build in accordance with V.L.A. standards and to accept supervision to assure the following of these standards.
(6)	The veteran to be given a contract to build at a price not to exceed 80 per cent of the value of the lot and completed house.
(7)	The director to undertake to advance money when work is completed by subcontractor or material is supplied to site, up to a total of, but not exceeding 75 per cent of the appraised value of the structure as it stands, and the material on the site at the time such payment is made.
(8)	Payments to be authorized by the V.L.A. construction supervisor on bills approved by the veteran-contractor direct to subcontractor or supplier of material.

The Address-Mr. Herridge
(9)	The lot and completed house to he sold to the veteran at the contract price-
My time has nearly expired, Mr. Speaker, but I do suggest that the Canadian Legion, in putting forward these proposals on housing, has made a very constructive suggestion toward the solution of the question of housing in so far as veterans in this country are concerned.
In concluding I must say that in this group we believe that large numbers of Canadians will be housed unsatisfactorily for years to

come unless we treat the question as a national emergency and use national credit to build the houses that are necessary if we are to have a happy, healthy and contented nation.
